speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Mr. STANLEY KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre) moved for leave to introduce a bill to amend the Judges Act.

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES IN OFFICE AFTER REACHING THE AGE OF SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES IN OFFICE AFTER REACHING THE AGE OF SEVENTY YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill
would add a new subsection to section 28 of the Judges Act, which is chapter 105 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927. The authority for legislation such as that proposed in this bill is to be found in section 100 of the British North America Act.
The purpose of the proposed addition is to provide that any judge of a superior court of any province or of the Yukon Territory who continues or is continued in office after attaining the age of seventy shall have his salary reduced to an amount equal to that which he would receive by way of retiring allowance if he were retired at seventy, less any sum which he might receive from a provincial government by way of other remuneration. The new salary rate would commence when the judge attained the age of seventy years, or on the first day of September, 1946, whichever is the later date. In the case of a judge appointed prior to the passing of the bill who would not be entitled to a retiring allowance if retired at the age of seventy, the operation of the act would be postponed until he is eligible for a retiring allowance.
This bill is similar to one which was passed by the House of Commons on May 10, 1933, but which was rejected by the senate. Apart from the effective date, the bill is exactly the same as the one passed by this house in 1933, but for two differences. In the first place the former bill stipulated seventy-five as the age at which provisions of that bill were to apply, whereas this bill stipulates the age of seventy. Secondly, the former bill made an exception in the case of judges not eligible for retiring allowance at the stipulated age whether appointed before or after the passing of that bill. In this bill the same exception is provided, but only in the case of judges appointed prior to the passing of this bill.
I may say that this bill is offered as a reasonable way of effecting a desirable change pending amendment of the British North America Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: This question is framed in such a way that an exact reply is difficult. The reason plumbing fixtures are not taken out of a building as soon as it has ceased to be used is that it is first necessary to determine the future use of the building, and whether the plumbing will or will not be required in that building to meet such future use. There is the further obvious fact that not everyone can be empowered to sell government property. Machinery has been set up for the sale of government property through War Assets Corporation and all sales are centred in that corporation.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
In view of the fact that the
minister made a statement on introducing the resolution a few days ago, I think perhaps I should make a brief statement now before second reading is given, in order that our attitude may not be in doubt.
The bill before us has for its purpose the extension of transportation by air within and outside Canada. In the earlier stages of the bill the minister made clear the government's position on air transportation. I hope I have not misunderstood the provisions of the bill or . the government's attitude towards the question.
At the outset of my very brief remarks may I say I recognize that this is a government bill and that the government, having a majority in the house will see that it is passed. I have therefore no intention of delaying it in any degree, and I am not hopeful that we can secure any modification of it. Under the

Trans-Canada Air Lines
circumstances I shall content myself with a brief statement setting out what I believe to be the weaknesses of this measure.
The bill, in the light of the minister's statement, is aimed to accomplish the expansion of mainline and international air transportation under government sponsorship, by practically denying private enterprise any share of either, and by risking the taxpayers' money in a government monopoly in these fields.
In my opinion this legislation will have five unfavourable results:	(1) it will discourage private enterprise in the whole field of civil aviation in Canada; (2) it will prevent private enterprise from serving efficiently the ' outlying communities of Canada; (3) it will extend state monopoly in this field to include international lines as well as trans-Canadian lines; (4) it will eventually drive the government into the position of subsidizing branch lines and thereby increasing the tax burden of the Canadian people; (5) it will eventually result in a huge state' monopoly with no competition to keep it efficient.
Our attitude with respect to this matter is the same as it is to other public enterprises of a similar character. It can be stated in two sentences: First, government owned projects such as this" must be encouraged and supported wherever and whenever they can serve the public interest best or improve the service already given. Second, monopoly, whether state owned or privately owned, in the field of transportation, should be discouraged, and competition, wherever practicable, should be encouraged if we are to ensure greater efficiency and therefore better public service.
I feel sure that all members of this house subscribe to the principle that Trans-Canada Air Lines must be made an efficient service. Certainly I do. To make it the most efficient service in the world might well be our legitimate goal. But we have had in the past [DOT] a tradition of competition in the field of enterprise in this country. Many of us believe it has had an important bearing on our economic development. The people of Canada, particularly the farmers of Canada, have been as much opposed to a public monopoly of the railway system as to a. private monopoly. They want neither private nor public monopoly. They want the two lines. This gives the man who travels or pays freight charges a chance to measure the efficiency of one against the other. In the light of this tradition let us examine what is happening to our air services.
By the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act passed in 1937 and since amended, the Canadian government went a long way in the direction
of giving over the air services of Canada to a state monopoly. When bill 21, now before us, becomes, law, we shall have gone a great deal farther along the same road. The fact that this is done by indirect as well as by direct methods makes the result none the less inevitable.
The practical effect of the legislation passed in previous years is that the government has been given power virtually to incorporate any feeder or subsidiary lines into the Trans-Canada air service organization. This power is a constant threat to those already engaged in the industry or who may wish to engage in it.
It is not only what the government has done under the present legislation that matters. The trouble is that the government's policy, and especially the minister's statements, keep those who are trying to develop air services under private management in a constant state of suspense and fear. No enterprise, public or private, can function efficiently under such conditions. If this state of uncertainly continues, private enterprise will be driven from the field. Meanwhile, the pilots and others working for the private systems do not know what their future is going to be. The fear is that the public system will become an octopus. It goes without saying under such conditions the private lines will be gradually absorbed by the government system or taken over by government-encouraged, subsidiaries.
I see no reason why a public air service especially with the resources of the Dominion of Canada behind it, should have any fear of its own ability to succeed on equal terms with its competitors, just as the Canadian National Railways compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway. If the power of parliament is to be used to destroy all competing services, then I say parliament is allowing itself to promote mbnopolistic policies. Such policies are in direct contrast to the principles of competition under which the great British merchant marine was developed, and under which the United States has grown to such power and influence. Such policies lead not only to a socialized state, but to all the inefficiencies that monopoly, particularly state monopoly, brings in its train.
In its present form, bill 21 extends the same dangerous principle into the field of international air transportation. The great majority of the members of this house, I believe, are opposed to adopting a policy by which all air services, external as well as domestic, are to become a state monopoly. I do not argue that we should have a second external air service to-morrow, but I think
Trans-Canada Air Lines

it is very shortsighted on the part of this government to announce to the world that is it practically foreclosing the possibility of a second service developing within the predictable future. I sincerely hope that-, on further consideration, the minister will state that this is not the government's intention.
I respectfully suggest also to the minister that before this bill comes out of committee the government incorporate in it a clause which will remove the fear of companies being taken over once they show any sign of becoming profitable. Before companies now in existence, and those that may later be formed, can be expected to expand or improve their services, they must have confidence that so long as they operate efficiently and give the best practicable service they are not going to be arbitrarily taken over cvr expropriated or without cause divested of the ownership and operation of their properties.
In the past few months there has been more talk by this government about encouraging private enterprise than we have heard for some years. I ask in all fairness, is this nothing but talk? In the face of legislation such as this, there is grave doubt that the government really intends to permit any private enterprise in this field. And if it is to be driven out of this field, what assurance has it that it will not be driven out of others?
The eyes of all Canada, particularly of Canada's youth, are to-day on the future prospects of this country. If this parliament is going to divert young and enterprising Canadians from seeking opportunities to develop their own lives and their own chances of getting on in their own chosen occupations in Canada, it will certainly add to its own future burden. If this parliament is going to discourage private enterprise, it is simply asking everybody to look for a government job.
I make these observations with all deference, because I feel it is important that this legislation do no more damage to private enterprise than necessarily follows from the provisions of the measure itself. As I said in the beginning, our attitude with respect to this matter is the same as it is with respect to other public enterprises of a similar kind. Government owned projects such as this must be encouraged and supported wherever and whenever they can serve the public interest best or improve the service already being given. Monopoly, whether state-owned or privately-owned, in the field of transportation should be discouraged, and competition, whenever practicable, should be encouraged if we are to ensure greater efficiency and therefore better public service.

As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, we have no desire to delay further consideration of this measure, but in view of the direction [DOT]in which this kind of legislation is leading us I thought I should make this brief statement before the measure becomes law.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the statement of the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) that a lengthy debate at this stage ought not to be necessary, and in that position we have been joined by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) by virtue of the fact 'that his remarks were brief. I rise , to make a few comments principally because of some of the things the previous speaker said.
First I want to say that I do not think we on this side of the house should make the statement that because the government has a majority of the members here all their legislation necessarily will carry in exactly the form in which it is brought down. There have been occasions this year when modifications have been made, and I can remember occasions in the last parliament, even when the government had a terrific majority, when government legislation was modified. So I feel [DOT]that on second thought the leader of the opposition will agree with me that there is reality to the discussions which take place in this chamber and that there is always a chance of our securing at least slight changes in the legislation which is brought down. In any case I would hope that we might gear our efforts to that end.
The leader of the opposition has made it fairly clear that he and his party are opposed to this bill, whether or not they intend to vote against it. In outlining the reasons for his opposition, if I heard him correctly, the hon. gentleman suggested three points. First he suggested that this bill was designed or'at least would have the effect of discouraging private enterprise in the -field of air transport. His second contention was that it would lead to ah increase in the tax burden upon the Canadian people, and the third point was that we were just heading toward another state monopoly, which in itself was a bad thing. I want to deal very briefly with each of these suggestions.
In these attempts to sing the praises of private enterprise, particularly when we are discussing transportation, my hon. friends are trading on the fiction that private enterprise by itself built up the railway systems of this country. I believe hon. members generally are conscious of the fact that the history of our Canadian railways does not bear out that suggestion; that our railways were given all

Trans-Canada Air Lines
sorts of assistance in the form of land grants and cash subsidies, and that they are still receiving assistance in the form of tax relief across this country. The plain fact of the matter is that the Canadian people have paid very heavily for every mile of railroad that has been built in this country, and I do not join at all in the paeans of praise which are sung to private enterprise on that score. The same thing is true in connection with air transport. The leader of the opposition paid a well deserved compliment to T.C.A. on their efficiency, and that implies a compliment to the government and to the Minister of Reconstruction on the job that has been done in building up this very efficient system, which is second to none anywhere else in the world. The fact also is to be noted, as we have tried to indicate a number of times in the debate on civil aviation, that huge government sums have been spent in building airports, in establishing meteorological services, beams and other aids to aerial navigation, all of which repeat the story we had with our railways. It is a story of the Canadian people putting their own money into the building of this new form of transportation.
The second charge against the bill made by the previous speaker is that it will increase the tax burden upon the Canadian people. There I feel that my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party are revealing the fact that they are living in a bygone age. They are thinking in terms of government as a body that should do as little as it can, spending as little money as possible. My understanding of government in this day and age is that it represents the collective effort of the people of the country as a whole to do in a cooperative way the things they could not do individually. Certainly we did not fight the war by a collection of private enterprise efforts. We fought the war as a people under the leadership of a government; and more and more this government, despite the fact that I find myself fighting it bitterly on many points, is yielding to the pressure of events and to the demand of this twentieth century that governments step into such fields as housing, for example, which we are discussing under another bill now on the order paper; transportation, and so on, to give service to the Canadian people. This continual cry for the spending of less money is completely out of step with the times. I would support my hon. friends in any effort they might make to curtail extravagance or wasteful expenditure, but as far as the mere shibboleth that you should not spend money is eoncarned, I suggest they are living in a bygone age. One of the jobs of government is to provide services, and one of
the things especially to the credit of T.C.A. and the job the government has done in building it up is that it is providing a service to our Canadian people which is enriching our life not only materially but in other ways as well. So I am not impressed at all with that argument.
The other argument advanced by my good friend, who comes from my province, where we have a number of public enterprises, was that we are setting up another state monopoly. There again I feel that my hon. friend is trading on a word. The word "monopoly'' in some connections has a very bad connotation, and apparently to use it is felt by my hon. friends to damn anything to which you apply it. But some things are natural monopolies. The postal service is something you would not suggest turning to a number of' private enterprises. So when you get into a highly specialized field such as air transportation we are satisfied that it is a natural monopoly and that as such it should not be in the hands of private individuals but should be run for the best interests of the people as a whole. My hon. friend used a phrase something like this. He said the power of parliament was being used to destroy competing services.
I want to tell my hon. friend that in so far as the minister obtains the power of this parliament to destroy the power of private agencies that are exploiting the people of Canada, all power to him. The power of parliament is not something which is being exercised against our people by some outside agency. The power of parliament is the people themselves attending to their own affairs. To the extent that the government is moving in this direction, I am happy as a member of the opposition to support them in the bill now before the house, and I take the strongest exception to the view expressed this afternoon by the leader of the Progressive Conservative party.
During 1944 and 1945 we have had a good many hours of discussion in the house on the question of civil aviation. Last year, throughout a number of stages of a number of measures, we had discussions, almost ad nauseam, on the subject, so that really it ought not to be necessary to discuss the matter at length on second reading to-day. I think I must point out, however, that despite the hours we have spent in discussion of this matter we have not yet had a clear statement from the Progressive Conservative party as to where it stands.
Without handing any bouquets to the government, I may point out that their position is clear. Our position, too, is clear beyond doubt. The government's position is
Tram-Canada Air Lines

that the main transcontinental services of this country shall be a complete monopoly of Trans-Canada Air Lines, and it takes the further position that all external lines shall be government controlled; they are to be operated by subsidiaries of Trans-Canada Air Lines. The government takes the further position that it may from time to time, through the governor in council, designate other routes in Canada, for government operation, and incorporate them into Trans-Canada Air Lines.
That is as far as the government goes in its domestic policy, with this exception: I feel it has admitted by its action' that it is prepared to be pressed along by events. By the policy it announced on March 17, 1944, it faced up to the monopoly which Canadian Pacific Air Lines was establishing, and in due course we are to have a divesting order so far as the air lines owned by the railways are concerned. Thus far the government has not said it will take over those feeder lines and incorporate them into a crown company. But the gradual designation of one line here and another there, and the simple fact that it will not be possible for a smaller company or individuals to take those lines over, makes it clear to me at any rate that in due course the government will have to take the position this group has advocated, namely, of incorporating those feeder lines into a national air system.

The government has not indicated that it is willing to go on and take over the feeder lines in Canada, but my contention is that the development of events will lead them in that direction-and my hon. friends to the right are quite justified in expecting that that is what is going to happen. The difference between the government and the C.C.F. on this point is that we do not just sit back and vait for these things to develop. We advocate that this should be done, that air transportation is a natural monopoly, that it is a field in which the interests of airmen are particularly at stake, and in which the interests fMr. Knowles.]

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
That is a pretty fair
ground for suspicion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
No doubt hon. members across the way realize there is a measure of truth in what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver South, namely, that the government's aviation policy is moving in the direction of socialism, and it is our contention that the pressure of events in this fast-moving age, which is calling for an ever and ever higher standard of living for our people, is calling for just this sort of thing. I hope that this bill will be supported not only by the government itself but whole-heartedly by its own back-benchers. The leader of the opposition said that he had no hope of seeing this bill delayed or modified, but the fact of the matter is that unless the government supporters are behind their minister on this bill, something might happen to it, and so I appeal to the supporters of the govermment to stand solidly behind this measure.
With all that I have already said on behalf of this party both last year and this, I think our position is quite clear, and that there is not much more that needs be said, except this. When we were in committee on the resolution preceding the bill I asked the minister whether the subsidiary companies to be set up under the bill would be confined to flying external routes, or whether they might be given contracts for flying some of the feeder routes within Canada, and his reply was that he would have to consult his lawyer after looking at the terms of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me to correct him, I do not think that was his question. His question was, could we under this legislation form subsidiary companies to operate in Canada, and I said that before saying whether we could or not I would have to consult the departmental solicitor, but at the same time I said that we had no intention of doing so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
That is correct. I accept the minister's correction as to the way in which I put the question. But I would point out to him that section 25, subsection 1, reads as follows:
The governor in council may authorize the minister to enter into a contract with any corporation incorporated under section twenty of this act, for the organization, operation and maintenance of air services designated from time to time by the governor in council.
I am not one of those lawyers or solicitors to whom the minister may refer, but it seems to me that the wording of that section is very clear and that the government could
Trans-Canada Air Lines

enter into a contract with one of these companies for operating an air service within Canada. I hope that when this bill becomes law and the government is faced with the pressure of events confirming what we have said, it will take the further step of enlarging ' the field of government control of air transportation to cover not only external but internal commercial flying within Canada on a much wider basis than, is now the case.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I do not argue that we should have a second external air service to-morrow, but I think it is very shortsighted on the part of this parliament"-I think I used the word government before-"to announce to the world that it is practically foreclosing the possibility of a second service developing within the predictable future."

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
The minister sometimes has peculiar ideas of the way we do things in the house, and the attitude he now takes as comfMr. Knowles.]
pared with the attitude he took the other day is along that line.
Before the bill goes to the committee there are one or two features of it which I think should be pointed out to the house. I rise not to attempt in any way to reply to the challenge thrown out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) or to enter into debate with him, but simply to deal with certain features of the bill. It is very easy for him and his party to take a clear-cut stand on this bill because they believe in the socialization of all means of transportation in Canada, and that includes, in my opinion, not only the airways but also the railways and shipping and the bus routes. He and his party are all-out for socialization of all means of transportation, I do not believe that the majority of the Canadian people want socialization along this line. In fact I am sure that a very small minority of the Canadian people believe in a policy of that type.
I think that the private members on the government side of the house have indicated their wisdom in being just a little reluctant to show any enthusiasm for the policy that has been announced by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, not only this year but also last year. The same attitude on their part was apparent last year. Obviously the Liberal members were not keen about the government's air policy; at least, they showed very few signs of keenness.
Coming to the bill itself, I do not think anyone can question the wisdom of giving Trans-Canada Air Lines power to increase their capital. The world is moving along; there have been great developments in the air, and money is required. Personally I think it was a wise move for the government to provide for an increase in capital. That provision is contained in the first section of the bill.
Another feature which is interesting is contained in the second section, which provides that the Canadian National Railway Company is to acquire this new capital, this additional $20,000,000 of capital. Of course that company already has the $5,000,000 authorized by the original bill, and now is to get an additional $20,000,000. Yet, as the minister stated the other night, in only a matter of a few months the Canadian National Railway, like the Canadian Pacific Railway, is to be forced out of the air picture. The Canadian National Railway will be covered by what the minister calls the divesting order, and when that is done, then under section 11 the shares of Trans-Canada Air Lines will all be held by the minister as a trustee for the crown. So that in considering this bill the

Trans-Canada Air Lines
members should keep in mind that the minister will be the sole shareholder of Trans-Canada Air Lines within the next six months. The Canadian National Railway will have no interest in Trans-Canada Air Lines. The accurate picture to be given to the Canadian people to-day is that of the' Minister of Munitions and Supply holding all the shares of Trans-Canada Air Lines within the next few months.
The main principle of the bill is contained in sections 10 and 3. Section 10 gives the governor in council power to create new government corporations. It is true that the shares of these new corporations are to be turned over to Trans-Canada Air Lines. In other words, Trans-Canada Air Lines is to have full control of these subsidiary government corporations. But the bill goes further: it gives the government power to subsidize these new government corporations. It is not only a question of how much money is to be put up for Trans-Canada Air Lines; there is also the power to subsidize the new corporations direct. And section 10 does not confine these new companies to international flying. The minister said the other day and repeated to-day that these new corporations would fly only on international routes, yet section 10 is in such terms that a new corporation could be set up by the government to fly domestic routes only. Surely if the government policy i3 that these corporations shall be set up to fly only international routes, the bill should give them power to go only that far; there should not be this additional power given, when the minister claims that it is not the policy of the government to set up new corporations to fly in the domestic field.
Section 3, which is the other key section of this bill, is much the same. It gives Trans-Canada Air Lines the power to acquire shares of these new government corporations, but there is no limitation to dealing with corporations flying outside of Canada. Under section 3 Trans-Canada Air Lines could acquire shares in a company set up solely for flying within the boundaries of- Canada, and I suggest to the minister that an amendment should be brought in to that section which would add, at the end of new subsection (e) the words "outside of Canada". I believe that when he made his statement that these powers were to be taken to deal only with international flying, he meant that, and if he did, surely the bill should read accordingly. If [DOT] the change I suggest were made, the power would be-

to purchase, hold, and, subject to the provisions of this act, sell and dispose of shares in any company incorporated under section
twenty of this act or in any company or corporation incorporated for the operation and maintenance of air lines or services of aircraft of any kind outside of Canada.
Without those qualifying last three words Trans-Canada Air Lines can acquire shares in any company whatever doing flying solely in Canada, and incidentally it could also acquire shares in a United States company which might be flying into Canada. I think this section should be given further consideration by the government.
Under the bill as it stands, Trans-Canada Air Lines could acquire all domestic lines. That is a very far-reaching policy. The minister says he has no intention of doing it. Well to make sure, let him change the bill so tha the power is not taken to do that.
Another feature of the bill is that it increases the powers of the minister and of the government. Under the present section 15, subsection 1, provision is made that there shall be what is known as a trans-Canada contract. Trans-Canada Air Lines was directed to enter into a trans-Canada contract with the minister. Now of course the position will be that the minister, as the sole shareholder of Trans-Canada Air Lines, will be contracting with himself as the minister-showing the anomalous position Into which the government is getting itself on this question. Then, under the present section 15, subsection 2, specific directions are given as to what this trans-Canada contract shall contain, and they are very important, for example, in paragraph (a) provision must be madefor the operation of the aforesaid lines of aircraft between points and over routes to be designated from time to time while the contract is in force by the governor in council.
The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but my understanding of that provision is that if Trans-Canada Air Lines is to take over a route and make that a main route, it must be designated as such by the governor in council. That is as the law stands at the present time, and it is a very important provision.
The contract must contain other terms, such as a schedule of services, tariffs, the furnishing of adequate equipment and of service, operation and maintenance of landing fields, and so on. I will not take the time to review them, but there are set out in this section special matters which must be dealt with in the Trans-Canada contract; they were considered in 1937 to be of sufficient importance to have them set out in the bill. But now,
Trans-Canada Air Lines

under the present bill, blanket power is given to the governor in council to make a contract without any of these provisions. Perhaps the minister did not mean it to read that way, and if he did not, I suggest that he ask the committee to amend the bill. He will find in section 6 of the present bill these words:
The first line of subsection two of section fifteen of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(2) The Trans-Canada contract shall contain such terms as the governor in council may order, and in the absence of such order shall provide,-"
-and then it will fit in to pick up the terms of the original act to which I have just referred. That means that the governor in council can make a contract which contains none of these terms or which contains only a portion of them. There is a wide-open power given to the governor in council. I suggest that that is a move in the wrong direction; in any event the minister should explain why that additional power is being taken. In reality it gives the governor in council a blank cheque; and that means, for all practical purposes, giving the minister a blank cheque. For example, under that provision he could get away from the need of designating points and routes which are to be flown by Trans-Canada Air Lines; if that blanket power is to be retained, some provisions should be put in the new bill to show just what additional terms the government have in mind as being possible in these contracts.
This is another example of framework legislation. The house is asked to pass the framework and then the minister fills in all the walls and covers the roof. It is not right; the government should bring in this legislation complete and not ask us to pass just a skeleton on which the minister can put the flesh.
Under section 10 of the bill there is to be a new section 25 of the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act. Here again we find that the governor in council is given the power to authorize the minister to enter into a contract with these new government corporations which are to be set up. In other words, the minister can enter into a contract with these new corporations quite regardless of Trans-Canada Air Lines. He can deal direct with a new corporation, and he is given the power in that same section to subsidize these same corporations direct without having the subsidy go through Trans-Canada Air Lines. I do not understand why that was done. There may have been some very good reason, but I suggest that the minister should explain that also, and give consideration to providing that any subsidies which are to be paid should be

paid to Trans-Canada Air Lines rather than go to half a dozen different subsidiary companies.
It is all just one more step towards making the minister the dictator of aviation in Canada. It may be that he is the man in Canada best qualified to be dictator of aviation, but on this side of the house we do not believe in dictators. I do not suppose my hon. friends to the left would have any objection to having a dictator of aviation, a dictator of railways, a dictator of shipping, but the official opposition believe that is a move in the wrong direction. It is bad enough in war; it is intolerable in peace. No such power should be given any one individual.
Finally, a fe.w words about branch lines or feeder lines. There was some confusion in the discussion the other day as to which was which, but all members will understand what I mean when I use those two expressions. The minister said the branch lines and feeder lines were to be left to private enterprise. They include of course the lines into the north country, and the routes that will take in all the intermediate cities even on the present main line. One instance given was the route from Vancouver to Kamloops, to Revelstoke and Calgary. Lines of that type are included in the group to which I wish to refer to-day, and they are of vital importance.
There is no doubt the main line is the most important, but these other lines are also of vital importance. Take the lines from Vancouver into the Yukon, from Edmonton into the Yukon, from Edmonton into the Mackenzie river district, and from Montreal up the north shore of the St. Lawrence. These lines come within this group, and they are of the utmost importance. Now there is great demand to connect up cities by air lines; it will not be long until they too are of great importance, and they should be given every encouragement. Nothing should be put in the way of the development of lines of this type. Help should be given not only to the present companies but also to new ones; Canada cannot afford to have efficient operations of that type destroyed or handicapped.
I believe that the move of the government in forcing the railways out of aviation is having that effect. The minister has never been able to satsify me that he had good reasons for forcing the railways out of aviation. It seems to me there is something of spite work, something of that type behind that move. I do not believe it was sound government policy-just a little more of the dictatorial attitude of which we have seen quite a bit during the last few years.

Trans-Canada Air Lines
Here we have Canadian Pacific Air Lines fiying now into the Yukon and giving efficient service. The minister said the other night that he will now have an international route from Whitehorse into Fairbanks in Alaska but will not have Trans-Canada flying it. He has sublet that run to the Canadian Pacific Air Lines. Does that not show you the whole picture? That it is an efficient line? No one can question that fact, certainly no one who has travelled on the line. They are good enough to be given the right to fly from Whitehorse to Fairbanks on behalf of Trans-Canada Air Lines, but in a few months' time the minister will say, "Now you have to divest yourself of this line and the Canadian Pacific Air Lines has to be broken up." It means the breaking down of a good system.
There is some talk by members of the C.C.F. about Canadian Pacific Air Lines having picked up a lot of bankrupt companies. Actually the main company they picked up-and here again I ask the minister to correct me if I am wrong-was Canadian Airways Limited, a company which had been doing a great deal of pioneer work and which was more or less the leading air pioneer in Canada. At one time it was destined to fly the Trans-Canada route. It was a company that was backed by the late James Richardson of Winnipeg, to whom Canadians owe a great debt of gratitude for the interest he took in aviation. When he died his interest in Canadian Airways Limited was taken over, and that is the way in which the Canadian Pacific acquired Canadian Airways Limited. So that the members of the C.C.F. have not been entirely accurate in making the sweeping charges they have made in their anxiety, or their eagerness, rather, to destroy the system.
I suggest to the minister that the result of his policy may very well be, as my leader has said this afternoon, that strong new companies will never be formed or never survive. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is very hopeful about that. He boasted to-day, just as he boasted last week, that this government's policy was making it impossible for there to be any strong air company in Canada other than Trans-Canada Air Lines, and if that happens, the responsibility will be right back on the doorstep of the present minister.
The probable end of this government policy will be that the government will have to step in and subsidize a lot of weak companies trying to operate these feeder lines and branch lines. The treasury of Canada will be called in to back up a lot of lines that have not had a fair chance to succeed. The result may also be inefficiency in the flying of these routes,
and almost certainly it will mean failure to expand in the branch line field as Canadians would otherwise expand. The policy in reality, is half-hearted socialism-half-hearted socialism, I repeat-and I advise private members on the government side to let that sink in and to realize where this policy is leading them.
Canada can lead the world in aviation. Our young men have led the world in flying both in the last war and in this war. We had a splendid record for flying these bush operations before the present war. Canadians take naturally to the air. The government should encourage-I hear an hon. member to my left muttering something. I would say it is the C.C.F. who are up in the air most of the time. I was about to say, the government should encourage all types of aviation development. It should encourage Trans-Canada Air Lines; it should give them every encouragement; that is why I am delighted to see that their capital is to be increased. It should encourage all companies flying the branch lines and also the bush pilots. We must have a bold air policy in this country, and the policy of the government at the present time is not a bold one. It is a policy of drastic bureaucratic control, entirely out of line-and this is the sad feature of the policy-with the initiative and the independent spirit of the individual Canadian.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: This afternoon we have heard from the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), as we heard last week when the resolution was before us, a great deal about the danger from dictatorship and monopoly and the absence of competition in the field of aviation. We hear references to the part played in transportation by the Canadian Pacific Railways, and more recently by the Canadian Pacific Air Lines; but like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I am still waiting for some clear enunciation of aviation policy as we might expect it if we had a Progressive Conservative government in office.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Maybe you would have a good government.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Maybe you would not.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
I might mention that the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act was passed in 1937. The leader of the opposition at that time, who did not pose as a Progressive Conservative, had more progressive ideas with regard to aviation than the present occupant of that high office. Speaking on the Trans-Canada Air Lines bill, as reported at page 2211 and 2212 of Hansard of 1937, Mr. Bennett said:
Trans-Canada Air Lines

But I do now implore* the minister not to part with this property. To-night the field is clear. To-night no franchise encumbers the ground. To-night we stand in a position to create by act of this parliament an enterprise that will have complete control of aerial navigation between the Atlantic and the Pacific.
Then farther on he said:
I make this suggestion to the minister not because I can be said to be one of those who believe in public ownership and control, for I have not that reputation, but because I have found by grim experience that the condition that now exists in Canada with respect to railroads has arisen in consequence of the blunder we made. We cannot make a blunder if we keep what we have got; and what we have got to-night is control of the whole matter. It seems to me, therefore, wise to take initial steps to ensure that that control shall be retained by the action of this parliament, and if we desire later to terminate it or to part with it, we may do so through an act of this house and as a result of the intelligent expression of opinion by members of parliament.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext: Bennett was clear-cut.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
The minister who is
piloting this bill through the house correctly pointed out last year that in 1937 the Canadian Pacific Railways and the company referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), the Canadian Airways, did have a chance to come in on the ground floor and help to develop this important industry, but they did not have the imagination at that time to see the possibilities of transportation by air in such a few short years.
While the Canadian Pacific Railways apparently have some loyal friends in this parliament, they have not been clear-cut in outlining just what should be done at this stage in the history of the country.
I wish to support what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said in urging the government not to be disturbed by the calling of names. The Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) has been called worse names than a dictator of aviation. No one worries about the Postmaster General being called a dictator of the post office by our friends who are opposed to public ownership. The important thing to consider is, can the job be done better under public control than under private competition?
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) read a carefully prepared document this afternoon. As I listened to him I could scarcely believe that this was the voice of the former premier of Manitoba; and when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre interpreted one part of the statement it seemed pretty clear to me that the leader of the opposition was not very sure himself just what was contained in the statement of policy. I do hope

that at this stage in the world's history members of the house are not going to be confused by the picture of what has happened in the last one hundred years in the competitive-world. In modern transport by air it is-important for some authority to provide the runways, the meteorological services and all the other services that are necessary in modern flying; therefore I think that neither the leader of the opposition nor anyone else has any right, to cast doubt upon the efficiency of public ownership in the field of transportation.
Occasionally I run across Americans who use the Trans-Canada Air Lines services in travelling from New York to the west coast-of the United States, and I have never met one who had any criticism to offer of Trans-Canada Air Lines services. In fact as I gauge the consensus it is that T.C.A. is giving a service that is superior to anything found in that field on this continent. The Minister of Reconstruction has reason to be proud of the remarkable performance of the Trans-Canada Air Lines since the first act was passed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
And deserves great credit
for it, too.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Certainly. I might
mention in passing that I travelled by plane to Halifax a couple of weeks ago. While we were changing planes in Montreal I went in for a cup of coffee and happened to sit beside a pilot] I inquired whether he was taking us out on the flight to Halifax. He replied that he was going across the Atlantic in a few minutes on one of the T.C.A. planes. I said: "What time do you expect to be over there?-' He said, "Oh in time for breakfast." It was then about six o'clock on Friday night. I said "When do you get back?" He replied, "If nothing happen, I shall be back home on Monday night." He was taking off at six o'clock on Friday, would cross the Atlantic twice and be back home for supper on Monday night. This merely demonstrates the sort of thing that T.C.A. has been able to do in providing transportation within our country and across the Atlantic in such a short time. I hope that the private members on the government side are not going to be frightened by statements that this is a measure of socialism in the field of air transport.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
Before the motion carries I wish to ask a question. I do not know whether the minister would like to answer it now or not. If he does not, it will be quite all right. When I was home on Saturday last helicopters were flying over the

Trans-Canada Air Lines
city of Toronto. I believe they were advertising the victory loan. It recalled1 to my mind that a year or two ago-perhaps it is longer than that-the Toronto Transportation Commission applied, I believe, for a licence, or it was announced that they were to apply to the minister for a licence, for the privilege of flying these helicopter machines in suburban .areas. For instance, they indicated that they would operate a helicopter from Toronto to Peterborough, from Toronto to Hamilton, and from Toronto to other nearby centres. I see that a proposal is to come before the United States congress asking for a licence to fly a similar machine, perhaps in many parts of the United States. Will this bill prevent any private company, such as the Toronto Transportation Commission, which has done such a wonderful job so far as transportation is concerned, from flying these helicopter machines?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES   INCREASE OF CAPITAL-CREATION OF CORPORATION TO OPERATE SERVICES UNDER CONTRACT
speechtext:
There seems to be some misunderstanding about the nature of this bill. There is nothing in this bill to prevent anyone from doing anything, with the exception of Trans-Canada Air Lines itself. This is purely a bill relating to Trans-Canada Air Lines. It neither prevents competition with Trans-Canada nor prevents any private enterprise from flying anywhere, nor does it in any way affect the interests of any company in Canada except Trans-Canada Air Lines.
In reply to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) the flying of helicopters is governed by the Air Transport Act. There are several applications on file having to do with helicopters. As soon as the applicants can tell the air transport board exactly where they can obtain their equipment and when they will be able to undertake the service for which they are applying, their applications will receive consideration. At the moment there is no helicopter service anywhere of a commercial nature; therefore the helicopter problem is one for the future.
Perhaps I should say just a word about the debate. Trans-Canada Air Lines is not such an old company that a review of its history need be lengthy. It has been stated that the original act, which did not reach parliament but was under discussion there, did not provide for a public company but rather for a company composed of Canadian National Railways, Canadian Pacific railways and Canadian Air Lines; in other words it was to be two-thirds private interests and one-third public interest. The purpose was to combine the three strongest transportation interests in Canada for the purpose of carrying out what the government considered to be a big job.
My own purpose in sponsoring the bill was to have one strong aviation company in Canada, to do the important job of operating a service from coast to coast. That was the purpose, and it had nothing to do with entering into an experiment in socialization. The day before the bill was to be introduced I was advised that the Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian Air Lines did not wish to be partners in the transaction, though the resolution that was to precede the bill already was under discussion in the house. Therefore on very short notice the: bill was changed, and Canadian National Railways was given sole ownership of the air line. In the discussion in this house it was stated that the purpose had been to include the Canadian Pacific Railway and Canadian Air Lines as partners in owning the line. The opposition then took a stand exactly contrary to that taken by the official opposition to-day. Mr. Bennet, then leader of the opposition, objected strenuously to the government parting with any share in this valuable franchise, to private interests.

Trans-Canada Air Lines

it has been ever since. The purpose was to form a strong company to operate Canada's main transcontinental service. That purpose has been pursued, and to-day I think Trans-Canada Air Lines is a strong company. It was organized with a capital of $5,000,000, of which the portion actually taken up stands at $4,700,000. It has not only preserved its capital but has enlarged it. The actual capital assets of Trans-Canada Air Lines to-day I think stand at over $7,000,000 according to the balance sheet. Someone has said that I regard Trans-Canada Air Lines as my baby and insist on keeping it. Well, perhaps I do; I admit it. But if I do, it is for only one purpose, and that is, before I leave public life, to make Trans-Canada Air Lines so strong a company that in the very unlikely event of the people of this country putting any of the groups opposite into the seats of government, the line cannot be wrecked either by the friends of private interests or by the theorists who believe that all property should be publicly operated. I think that explains my position The purpose of this bill is to permit Trans-Canada Air Lines to enter a wider field. It is not the purpose to give the government any less control than it has to-day, but it recognizes the fact that in venturing into other countries we must recognize the laws of those countries, and thus we require a more flexible act in order to be free to do business there. That is the purpose of the bill. It is the intention to send it to the committee on government-owned railways and shipping, where the officers of Trans-Canada Air Lines will be present to answer any questions that may be put to them. The hon. member for Vancouver South has asked why certain paragraphs of the bill are expressed as they are. Those questions can be put to the officers of the company. If the replies are not satisfactory I have no doubt that committee will recommend to the committee of the whole that the bill be amended accordingly.
This has been an interesting discussion and I trust that the committee, which begins its sittings to-morrow, will be able to give further study to the bill and to satisfy hon. members as to the meaning of the amendments now before the house.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments on the rehabilitation and demobilization policy of the government, particularly as to the way in which it is working out to the disadvantage of men who served in actual theatres of war; that is, men who have had combat experience. The present point system, by which two points are given per month for service in Canada, and three points per month for service overseas, gives the man who has actually fought no advantage over a man who has spent his entire service at a desk in England, for example, and very little advantage over a man who has served most of his time, if not all of it, in Canada. However, with regard to those who are actually overseas, under this system the man who fought has not very much advantage over the man who served most of his time in Canada, and then went overseas for three months.
The original points system, which was put into effect under what we called the five-year plan, to give thirty days leave in Canada to men who had been overseas for five years, was a different system, and was designed to operate in favour of the men who had actually been fighting. Under the original system one point per month was given for service not in any theatre of war, and two points for service in a theatre of war. This meant that, in practice, a man could not get back to Canada for thirty days leave unless he had seen actual service in Sicily, Italy or northwestern Europe; in other words, unless he had been in an actual theatre of war. A man who had gone overseas in the fall of 1939, but who had spent all his service in England, did not get home under that thirty-day plan; at least he did not, up to the time I came home in April, under that plan.
This was a much fairer and better system than the one now in force. Why was it abandoned in favour of the present system under which a man who served in Canada for two or three years and then went overseas, too late to get into the fighting, has priority over a man who served a few months in
Demobilization-Army

Canada and then went overseas to go right into the fighting, and who continued in that fighting for probably four or five months, which is a long time in the life of an infantry soldier? The life of the infantryman is short.
A considerable number of men who served five or six months or more in actual fighting now find themselves in a position where men who never heard a shot fired have priority, so far as returning to Canada is concerned. There are a number of men in this category in the Canadian occupation forces in Germany, as is disclosed by the figures at page 603 of Hansard. These figures show that, as of September 1, 1945, there were 495 officers and 11,613 other ranks, volunteers for war in Europe, who were serving in the occupation forces against their will. Of these men, 4,622, all ranks, had served six months or more in a theatre of war, in- actual operations against the enemy. On the same date there were only 1,778 N.R.M.A. soldiers serving in the occupation forces.
When we compare these figures with those given in the editorial in the Ma-ple Leaf, which was read into Hansard by the minister a few days ago, we find that of the draft of the Saskatoon Light Infantry returning to Canada at that time, 30-1 per cent were N.RJM.A. personnel. Further on in the editorial there are cited four cases picked at random from among returning personnel of the N.RJM.A., not one of whom had ever been in action. Two of them had arrived in northwest Europe after hostilities -had ceased. In view of this, can one wonder that this editorial was written? It would have been surprising if it had not been written. Can this committee come to any other conclusion than that the men I have mentioned who actually fought and are now in the occupation forces have been discriminated against, dealt with unfairly, so far as their return to Canada is concerned, and naturally they are disgruntled-? Surely any reasonable system would send back to Canada the men who had been longest away from Canada. But this system has been doing just the opposite very often. It has been sending back to -Canada men who did not go to northwest Europe until the fighting there was all over, and it leaves in the occupation forces many men who had been over there and- fighting for six months or more. In other words, it is leaving a lot of men there who have -been away from Canada and away from their families much longer than many of the men who are being returned.
It is all very well for the minister and his officials at ND.H.Q. and C.M.H.Q. to institute this system and defend' it as fair and 
reasonable, but I should like, as one who has spent sixteen months over there fighting, to assure them that they can never justify it to the men who did -the fighting or -persuade them that it is a fair and reasonable system.
There is another group of men who are being unfairly discriminated- against. I refer to the- men who -have long service but who, because it is claimed they are still needed overseas or may be needed- because of their trades classification, or something along that line, are being retained over there instead- of being sent home. I am convinced that a very considerable number of these men are not actually holding key jobs at -all and could readily -be brought -home. I have a letter from one of these men which illustrates about as well as anything could exactly what is going on overseas at the present time. It illustrates the attitude of a lot of these men which is being engendered by the government's repatriation policy. This letter is from a sergeant and reads:
I have enclosed a copy of the Canadian forces overseas newspaper The Maple Leaf which contains an editorial that really and truly expresses the present opinion- of the high score volunteer personnel still overseas.
Personally I have 192 points. I came overseas in February, 1941. One year ago I wasn't wanted as a clerk so was sent on a number of N.C.O. & C.S.M. courses and qualified as Q-l with recommendation. I was promptly reverted to corporal and- conscripted for infantry training. Yalue of so-called conversion training received

nil. Arrived in Belgium early in February, 1945, and wtas informed that I could not be posted- [DOT]
He means posted- to an infantry battalion.
-because of my trade. Later was posted -to 1 Cdn. Spec. Vehicle Coy. in Mediterranean theatre as pay sergeant. Completion of the work there led me to ask for an -appointment where my previous experience would be of , value to the army.
I w^as posted to 3 Cd-n. NETD surplus to establishment as an attachment. During my stay at this unit from 18th May to date, I can- truthfully say there has been less than four weeks during which my service was really necessary.
I am firmly convinced that the boys who volunteered during the first two years are definitely being treated as expressed by the local adjutant to two of the boys, Who were paraded. They were told, "You volunteered too soon-you came overseas too soon, you gained too much promotion and you did too good a job-you have too many points and we still need you". They were employed playing crib an average of seven hours daily.
We all feel that if the present rate of return of low score men continues, a point "will soon be reached in the C.A.O.F., which will require that those of us high score personnel still overseas will be required to give additional service to fulfil Canada's commitment in Germany.
I sincerely hope that this will not cause you too much inconvenience and that you will be able to help us to get a square deal.

Demobiliza tion-A rmy
We are not suckers enough that the monthly increase being obtained in our idle service in the form of a gratuity is something for nothing. Eventually we will have to repay a large part of it in the form of various taxes.
There is a letter, one can tell from the tone of it, from an intelligent man and it shows quite well what is happening in a large number of cases. These men with long service are being kept there because they are supposed to be holding key jobs. Yet, the writer states that two of his pals are employed chiefly in playing crib. Before we pass these estimates the minister should make a statement telling us why and under what circumstances the present point system was adopted. From what I have said, it is clear that the present point system is different from the original system adopted, under which men were to be brought home for thirty days leave and which properly, I think, did give a preference to the men who had actually done the fighting.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have already given two explanations of the manner in which the present point system was adopted, and there is not much that I can add. I did it briefly in the debate on the address in reply to a speech made by the hon. member for Nanaimo, and I did it again, in more detail, in my extended remarks in presenting these estimates. Briefly, the system was worked out by General Crerar and his officers early in May and announced in a booklet that was distributed to the troops about May 10 or May 15. Subsequently another pamphlet was put out by General Simmonds early in September. Basically the principle has remained unchanged. It was worked out by the men on the spot who presumably knew the conditions. It was accepted by national defence headquarters in Ottawa as being the scheme prepared by the men in the best position to know what would be a sound scheme. The scheme is working and is working well, and I for one would not be prepared to make a change and bring about all the uncertainties and confusion and chaos that followed after the last war unless I were sure a change was necessary.
Why was the original plan abandoned in favour of the present? I have not seen any answer to that question in the minister's statement now or previously.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I can only answer that the present system was worked out and decided 47696-101
upon by competent officers whose names I have mentioned, men in the field in whose judgment I have confidence and- in whose judgment I am sure my predecessor had confidence.

I think the hon. member for Calgary East has raised some pertinent questions deserving a better answer than the minister gave.
There is another matter that has given me considerable concern. Returns have been brought down showing how many N.R.M.A. men have been returning with their units from overseas. The minister should give us a statement telling us in more detail who was responsible for that. When one thinks of all the ramifications we have had with our army, with our organizations, with our two-army system, throughout these years of war, and then comes to the period following V-E day and discovers that such great numbers of these N.R.M.A. men were attached to the first division, for example, although they were with it only after the combat was finished in the European theatre of war, it is evident that somebody must have been responsible for that system. Great numbers of men with a very low number of points were attached to the first division following the cessation of hostilities, although everybody responsible for it must have known that those people, with that very low-point system, would be among the first to return with these units to Canada. It is matter of fact that great numbers who never saw active combat are being returned with those units, and on the other hand there are many cases of long-service personnel who are retained overseas, apart from those cases which have been pointed out. I know of a married man with a family who has been five years overseas, has served in an actual theatre of war, and certainly would like to return to this country, but who is now retained with the army of occupation. Considering the working of this whole system throughout the years of war and up to the present, and seeing what is happening under it, I think we are entitled to some more detailed explanation from the minister. Very great dissatisfaction exists. It is not a matter of isolated grievances. It has been pointed out that, of the present occupational army in Europe as of September 1, 1945, 4,622 of all ranks have seen six months active service or more. They are certainly retained there, against their own

Demobilization-Army

will; they have not volunteered for the job. The whole system is most unsatisfactory, and the fact that the minister says that the chief of staff organized all this, and that the government is satisfied with it, is not good enough for the people of this country at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I could fire the chief of staff, I suppose.
Some better explanation is required, because the government are responsible for the acts of the chief of staff.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: But the government must either accept the advice of its senior military officers or replace them. General Crerar was not the responsible officer during my time as minister. If he had been, I should have had the greatest confidence in him. I have the greatest confidence in the present chief of staff, in General Simmonds, and in General Vokes. All these men are, I think, doing a difficult task extremely well, and as long as I have confidence in them I must accept their advice as to what is the best method. I may query them as to particular points, but so far as my own limited knowledge of these matters is concerned I have not been able to see that the plan which they have worked out and which they recommend to me is an unsound plan, and until I am convinced that it is I intend to support it.

Is the minister quite satisfied that these long service men who have seen actual combat should be retained over there, and all these other chaps, many of whom have not seen active service, should be called back?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have explained all that two or three times. When my hon, friend speaks of a great number, I must tell him that there are comparatively few. I hope to quote to the committee the exact number.
I have said that there are 4,622.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Just allow me to make my statement, if you will. I will get the exact number before the committee rises and give the figures.
The Saskatoon Light Infantry was mentioned as having a large proportion of N.R.M.A. men in the number who came back with the first division. That is undoubtedly true. The Saskatoon Light Infantry had sustained fairly

heavy casualties. As, I believe, hon. members of the committee know, the policy is followed in the army of endeavouring to reinforce on a territorial basis. You try to get men from about the same area into a unit which needs reinforcement. I can only assume that available reinforcements from the area in which the Saskatoon Light Infantry had been recruited, at the time reinforcements were needed, were N.R.M.A. personnel, which would account for the large proportion of N.R.M.A. men in that unit at the time. As I have explained several times, the policy is that, first, we skimmed off the men with high-point scores who could be spared and they were sent back in Canada drafts. Then repatriation started by units, with units of the first division coming first. That movement has now been completed. In units of the first division men with fifty points and upwards came back with their units; men with less than fifty points were retained for further duty.
That is the policy. That is the policy which was laid down by competent officers overseas in whose judgment I have confidence, and until I can be shown by some higher authority that that is not a proper policy, that is the one we are going to follow. I repeat to the committee that nothing is perfect. We concede that in some places, perhaps, things could be improved. But the system is working, and working pretty well; and I will say that I am not so much concerned about the relatively light-point man who happens to get home with a draft of his unit; what I am concerned about is the really high-point man who is held over there on the ground that he is essential but who contends that he is not. I do not want to add to my already heavy correspondence, but if any hon. member will communicate to me the case of a high-point man who is held overseas on the ground that he is essential, I will look into it. He is the one I am concerned with. Frankly I do not care very much if a thousand or twelve hundred relatively low-point men get home with men of longer service. I do not think, viewing the picture broadly, that that is terribly important. I do think it is. important that the movement should be as fair, as orderly and as expeditious as possible. That is what we are trying to do; it is what the army staff are trying to do; and I am going to give them just as much support as I can to see that that is done. Let nobody think that I do not know the feelings of the man who is waiting over in England to be repatriated. As I told the committee the

Demobilization-Army
other day, I have only to recall my own experience. I waited in England from November, 1918, to June, 1919, and saw others going home. I did not know the basis on which they were being sent home, and thought I was the forgotten man. The basis which has been worked out in this war was made known to the troops as long ago as last May, and it has been explained to them since. General Sim-monds issued a further pamphlet, and as I am advised, it is now pretty well understood. I had a long memorandum from General Sim-monds the other day in which he reviewed the whole position.
I honestly believe that the system is working well, and I would be most reluctant to. admit that any radical change should be made in that system.

The thing that strikes
me is this. I asked what I thought was a fairly straight question, as to why this original point system was changed. The only answer I have had from the minister is that he has full confidence in the higher ranking officers overseas. That is not an answer to the question at all. Even if he has full confidence in the high ranking officers overseas I believe we are still entitled to know why the system is changed. If he does not know, he should ask his officers to give the information to him.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I asked why the system was changed. It was never changed as far as repatriation was concerned; it was changed as far as rotational leave is concerned. But my information is that the system was never changed. It was the system as originally announced after V-E day. There has been no change in the point score since then. Old soldiers will realize that, particularly in this war, it is very difficult to allocate points for active service. A man serving on the docks in Antwerp might be under a good deal heavier fire than the man who was serving up near the front line. Unfortunately I have not been over in this war, but I understand that in some parts of England they were not entirely free from risk on this occasion either.

To carry this matter a short distance farther, the minister said that this policy was based upon the advice of very high ranking officers whom he named, and he said that until they changed their opinion he was not proposing to go contrary to their advice. I wish to say, and I am sure I speak for everyone in the official opposition, 47696-101i
that we on this side of the house have every bit as much confidence in these officers as has the minister. We are not criticizing these officers in any respect. Some, of us served under some or all of them; no one who did so would ever dream of questioning their great ability to lead and the great service they rendered the troops of whom we are speaking, both while fighting and since, and I know they will continue to render that service.
I do not think, however, that that ends the matter. When that pamphlet was issued in Europe in May or at the end of April it represented a system which had not been tried out. Its imperfections, if there were any, had not revealed themselves in practice, and I am sure that the officers of whom we have, been speaking were never men of rigid mind but were always ready to make any necessary change in their original plans as the exigencies of the military situation demanded. The fact that that plan was devised in April and promulgated then does not relieve the government from the responsibility of changing it if in fact it has worked out to the serious disadvantage of any major class of troops overseas.
I think the plan should have been revised before when these matters first came up, but in any event it should be revised now. After all, there are still over one hundred thousand troops overseas. I have not the figure in front of me and it might be very much greater than that. Their return is not going to be achieved until March or April next.
The minister also said that he was sure the plan at the present time was understood by the troops over there; it had been explained to them, many times. I quite agree, and I realize of course the serious consideration which has to be given to the question of changing a plan which has been so clearly announced as that plan has been. But I suggest to the minister that, although that plan has been understood, it has not been accepted by the troops overseas as a fair one, and now the hon. member for Calgary East is asking that there be made in it an alteration the nature of which he has indicated.
The troops, we say, who have been, discriminated against by this plan-unintentionally discriminated against of course-are those with active service in a theatre of operation.. The suggestion we are making is that their point score be revised upwards so that they will get credit for their actual fighting and will come back ahead of those who did not actually fight. That will not cause a tremendous upheaval overseas; all it will
Demobilization-Army

do is to revise the point scores of fighting men, and if I know the soldiers overseas you will get little complaint from those who did not see actual fighting if their brothers in arms who fought get this advantage.
There is a certain soreness over there now and it is understandable.
