I suggest that the change proposed would not create another soreness but would only relieve the present one, and it is still not too late to make that change if the circumstances indicate that it should be done. I wish to bring to the attention of the house once more what the minister said at page 1131 of Hansard:
The common principle underlying the whole scheme of demobilization has always been, and in future will continue to be that, subject to the exigencies of the service and to the national interests, the personnel with the longest and hardest service should be given first opportunity to return to civil life.
I call attention to that word "hardest". These are the minister's own words; that is the principle we are urging now, and it is exactly the principle that is not recognized in the present point system. Show me a place in the present point system where there is any measure of hardness of service. None whatever. That change can be made now without causing bitterness, and that) is all we are asking.
There is one other thing I might say in an attempt to destroy the argument that the plan made last April should not be changed now and still stand's good. My recollection of that plan was that an important part of it consisted of the process of cross-postings so that troops with high points and coming from, say British Columbia, could be transferred into a British Columbia unit in a division with a high priority on coming home. That was a well-intended idea and was undoubtedly carried out to the best of the ability of the army overseas.
But cross-postings of large numbers of men are very difficult indeed, and it is certainly open for consideration now to wonder whether that process of cross-posting actually was achieved sufficiently well to ensure that the policy did not create a hardship, which in theory it was never intended to create and in theory perhaps would not have created.
I suggest to the minister that it is not too late to make that change, not too late to come back to the system of points for rotational leave. The whole question of points rather beclouds issues. You must have some kind of rule of thumb system so that you can make your *calculations, but it would perhaps have been much better if there had been no points at all, if it could have been done on the basis of bow long a man had been there and how hard

he had fought. By translating it into a question of points we have hidden the human side altogether, and I suggest that, in the proposals made from this side of the house, we have unearthed one of the important human issues about this matter. The point system should be rearranged to remove the hardship caused by its working out.

I would support the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard in this respect. I have written to the minister on a number of these cases, and while he has given every consideration to any case brought to his attention, as I can well testify, nevertheless I believe that the policy is working out in the manner indicated by the hon. rfiemiber. I Have looked through some of the letters which I have received from parents and from men in the services. So far as I can judge, one type of complaint boils down to this, that the low-point men who happened to be on the continent at the time the war ended were the men who very often had done the hardest fighting and were retained in the army of occupation. It seems to me that there is a defect in the present .point system.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You mean "high point". You said low point.

I mean precisely what I said, that the low-point men who happened to be on the continent and who had been engaged in the hard fighting leading up te the fall of Germany were retained in the army of occupation, while other men who had high points and who had not been in the actual theatre of war for any length of time, or any hard fighting, were returned home. That seems to be a difficulty in which the minister finds himself in regard to the present point system.
I looked over some of the considerable correspondence I have on this particular matter and I found some interesting criticisms that have been made from time, to time. Here is one. A boy enlisted voluntarily on January 1, 1943, on his eighteenth birthday, in the infantry service. In December, 1943, he was in action in the Mediterranean theatre. He was in the hospital subsequently with yellow fever, dysentery and malaria. On September 4, 1944, he was severely wounded and hospitalized. Later he again returned to battle in northwest Europe and was repeatedly in action. This lad who had undergone so much mental and physical strain was placed in the army of occupation. I believe this is a type of case that is causing some of the criticism which we are getting from outside the house, and which I sympathize with greatly.

Demobilization-Army
Here is another lad who joined the army immediately on completing grade 12. He served as an infantryman throughout a major part of the northwestern European campaign until he was wounded in April, 1945. At the present time he is attending the khaki university in England, and has just written his parents that he will be posted to the army of occupation. It seems to me that the point system does not cover cases of this description. I have before me too a letter from a young lad which is written in a strain that I very much regret to see in any letter from a Canadian boy overseas. I am not going to quote it all, but he says this:
The army has seen fit to post me to the army of occupation and I am to report as soon as possible. There is one other fellow from my company here, also slated to go with me. He is my pal. He is married and at home, and has five and one-half years' service overseas, which surely entitles him to be repatriated.
These are types of cases that are not met by the present point system; these are types of cases to which the minister needs to give some consideration. What the solution is I would hesitate to say, but I suggest that if we are to have a point system some special points might be given to enable cases of this kind, men who have done the hardest fighting, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said, to get back home. I do not know whether that is possible, but I am bringing the matter before the minister, because, as I said at the outset of these brief remarks, I have taken a number of cases to him in the last few weeks, and I have had the most sympathetic consideration. But it is not good enough that a member of parliament shall be approached by the parents or by friends or by the lad himself and then go to the minister and get the sympathetic consideration which we have received. That is not good enough. We need some policy
They should not have to go to a member.
No. A policy should be laid down which would obviate that necessity, and it is up to the minister and his staff to devise such a policy.
I have a few things I would like to say.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: May I make an explanation, because all these points are being considered.
I believe the minister said that no change is-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In principle.

Well, I have a letter here, a part of which I should like to read. It is dated September 29, and reads as follows:
About ten days ago the Maple Leaf appeared w.th headlines "All personnel down to 110 points will be repatriated by September 28", and now this letter comes through. Everywhere you go you hear the boys remark, "If they really wanted to get us home they could damn well find the shipping".
Here is the letter to which he refers. It is a circular letter No. 501, C.M.H.Q., dated September 27, 1945:	*
Canada Drafts
Personnel in United Kingdom with high point scores.
1.	Records circular letter No. 144 required a return to reach records office not later than September 18, 1945, of all officers and other ranks with point scores of more than 110 who would be available by September 18, 1945, for posting to Canadian repat depots between 26 and 28 September, 1945.
2.	Posting this personnel to repat depots between these dates would mean that, individuals would remain in the repat depots for approximately eight to ten weeks. In view of this long period in, the repat depot, it has been decided that such personnel will remain with their present units and postings to the repat depot will be made at a later date which will be advised, thus reducing the length of time the individuals are in the repat depots.
There is the trouble. In the Maple Leaf they said that those with points down to 110 would be repatriated before September 28.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It should not have said that.

That was what was in the Maple Leaf, but then this order comes out? to all those in the high-point scores that they must remain where they are, and I think that is where part of the trouble lies. This letter was issued by Major General Weeks. The' boys overseas were told by the Maple Leaf that they would get out. Then this letter tells them to stay where they are and they are pretty mad.

I can give the minister a few more points to answer, both in connection with, and apart from, the point system itself. The first point that I should like to deal with briefly is the question of responsibility for this policy. This point system was devised by senior officers overseas. I say in all seriousness that I am very glad indeed to hear the minister state that he has the utmost confidence in those senior officers, because I was afraid when this question was first discussed in the house that the minister did not have much confidence in them and therefore was going to leave them to take the whole responsibility for this policy. He did say then that this was devised by senior officers overseas and that they are responsible for it. I
Demobilization-Army

am glad to hear him say now that he accepted their decision and is going to support them. But at the same time I believe it does put us in a position, when criticizing this policy, of criticizing indirectly those very high ranking officers. Well, that is a thing which one must take into due consideration when criticiz-the policy. But we are still free to criticize the policy, and to point out, as was cogently observed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, that although General Crerar devised the policy, that was last May, and does not mean the policy is correct to-day or that it is working out to the advantage of the men who did the longest and hardest fighting.
There is no guarantee that the policy is fool-proof or incapable of being mistaken just because a high ranking and responsible officer has thought it out and devised it. We are suggesting in effect that the policy, no matter who initiated it or worked out the details, is not working out as it should and is actually inflicting hardship on the men overseas. I urge the minister to go one step farther and accept his ultimate responsibility by going back to these officers and saying, "All right; it may have been good, but I will accept my responsibility and require you to initiate the necessaiy changes."
In discussing this point system, whoever originated it, I think the fact should be borne in mind that, as has been so clearly proven by events, this policy is arousing the opposition, not to say the hostility, of men of all ranks overseas. This is borne out when we go back ' and consider what happened when the editor of the Maple Leaf was removed from his position. If it could be said that this dissatisfaction with the point system represented merely a certain amount of letting off steam we would be inclined to say that if the minister had investigated and was satisfied that it was all right, we would let it drop. But when the situation arises where the responsible editor of the army newspaper, who had occupied that position for fully two years, finds it necessary to take the serious step of defying his superior officer and resigning or being removed, thus coming into open- conflict with his general officer commanding, then I think we can take it as fairly well established that there is something behind the feeling he is trying to express. It could not have been merely his own personal opinion, or he would not have resigned his position; he would not have refused to publish the other article. I point out that he took violent and open issue; he found himself in the position of having to obey orders or say, "No. The matter is so serious I have to refuse to obey orders, though I know full well what will be the consequen-

ces." That was the decision taken by Major Macfarlane, and I think that should be indicative to'us of the seriousness of the situation. Not only did he take that step, but we find the same thing being done by the assistant editor, Lieutenant Ingraham. I am reading now from the Ottawa Journal of September 24:
Lieutenant Ed. Ingraham .	.	. assistant
editor of the northwest Europe edition of the Maple Leaf . . . said to-day he has "resigned on principle" following the removal of the editor. . . .
And a little further down:
Lieutenant-Colonel Gilchrist . . . called other members of the editorial and composing room staff to a meeting, and reminded them they were soldiers and- must d-o as ordered. But later half the compositors and make-up crews submitted requests for transfers.
I merely mention these two facts to show how seriously the men overseas regard the unfair working of this point system, which is bringing hardship to the men who have done the longest and hardest fighting. I do not think it necessary to emphasize or elaborate on the unfairness which actually is being done. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has shown in the few remarks he made that a man who joined toward the end of 1943 but who got into action almost immediately and fought continuously for a year or more, still might have fewer points than a man who might have come over from Canada only recently, or who might have been in England all the time, but because the first man had fewer points he was put into the army of occupation and wil-l be repatriated later than those men who never saw action. That view is not confined only to members on this side of the house. It is held) by men overseas and by men who have come back to this country. The minister must take account of that widespread and firmly held view, because it is causing such bitterness. It is not a matter in connection with which he can say, "there is a misconception on somebody's part, but the policy really is fair." I suggest that the soldiers are about the fairest judges of the minister's action-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt
my hon. friend-, because I have a perfectly open mind on this question, but some alternative policy must be suggested.
I was under the impression that -this had been done. If not, I will run over it again.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is what I want to
discuss. We -are dealing in generalities at the moment.

I will run over it again.

Demobilization-Army

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I should like specific suggestions as to how the point score should be changed.

I am glad to hear the
minister does not require much more proof that it is a serious matter, but I should like just to bring to his attention this last item perhaps to clinch the matter. I quote from the 'Vancouver Sun, a good Liberal newspaper, of October 9, 1945:
The "point" system of service credits, basis for release from the Canadian army, was the object of severe criticism among returning Seaforth Highlanders.
That regiment returned home at the beginning of this month.
The combat veterans of this crack battalion are "mad" about the system which they allege let men come back to Canada who "never fired a rifle in anger".	.
At the same time they charge many of their combat comrades from Sicily and Italy have been kept in northwest Europe on the Canadian occupational force.
Here is another paragraph I shall read to the minister without comment to show how serious they consider this matter to be:
One Seaforth who served through every Italian and northwest Europe campaign said that out of 260 Seaforths of the second section "not more than 100 should have marched with us, with our colours."
That is how the men returning feel about it; not the men still over there, anxious to get back, but men who have returned to this country, thinking of their comrades who should be back here but who are not.
The minister mentioned the case of the Saskatoon Light Infantry to which he said a number of men with low-point scores had been posted after V-E day. In justification for the fact that many of these men had been brought back to Canada, he said that this unit had suffered pretty heavy casualties and that it was necessary to send a great many replacements. I would be the last to minimize the job done by the Saskatoon Light Infantry, but that was the support battalion of the first division and its casualties were light by comparison, and by comparison only. If, notwithstanding that, a number of men who had not reached that battalion until after V-E day were returned with them-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend does not wish to be unfair, but that was not what I said. I said that they were not posted in order to be returned to Canada; they were posted in the ordinary course before or about Y-E day, on the regular basis of territorial posting and that months later, when the unit was ready to return to Canada, they came back with it. I am sure my hon. friend would
like to keep that straight, in fairness to the Saskatoon Light Infantry. The posting was not made in view of the return to Canada.

I appreciate the distinction, and I did not intend to put that slant on the ministers words. In any event these men were posted, and by virtue of the fact that they were with the unit and had a sufficient number of points, when the unit came to be repatriated they came back- with it. If these men were posted to the Saskatoon Light Infantry, which had comparatively light casualties, then a great many more must have been posted toother infantry regiments with heavier casualties, so that we are going to have a great many more men with little or no combat experience coming back, while we still keep over there men with a great deal of combat experience. The ministers own statement as to how that occurred in connection with the Saskatoon Light Infantry surely should show him on reflection the necessity for changing the basis on which men are repatriated from overseas, so that we may get back first those men who have done the longest and hardest fighting.
In connection with this matter of the retention of long service personnel may I point out that, as is indicated in the article dealing with the Seaforths, many of the men who, they feel, should be coming back, are posted to the army of occupation, while many others are kept in Europe on the basis of their being key personnel. The minister has said1-and I appreciate his point-that he does not wish to open up new files, but that if we will bring to his attention any case in which a hardship has been shown, he will see that it is given consideration.
I can say only this, that I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) when he says that there is a volume of cases being brought to the minister's attention sufficient to prove conclusively that a new approach is necessary, and that some new system should be evolved to prevent the necessity of referring all these cases.
One point which occurs to me, and which I shall suggest he should bring to the attention of officers overseas, is that they should revise their thinking when it comes to a matter of deciding as to the indispensability of personnel, because I know the tendency is, when one has a good and valuable man, to say that he is "key personnel" in order to avoid losing him, when, in fact, one may have no real basis for making that statement.
However, a number of cases in this category are coming to light. I know of two brothers who had been in the army for four and 4i
Demobilization-Army

years respectively, most of which time was served1 overseas, both of whom are cooks and are being kept on the ground that they are key personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Have they had combat experience?

Yes, insofar as cooks are able to get it. They were with combat units. In any event, I am wondering if the training of cooks was stopped two years ago, because surely there must be a number of cooks and other tradesmen in the NTtjM.A. personnel, and in other personnel, who were dispatched with the last drafts to leave Canada, and who could be available to replace those who are held out to be key personnel. If there are not, then the only assumption is that the training of tradesmen was stopped two years ago. Until I get that assurance from the minister, I cannot accept that. Therefore I suggest that he put up to his officers overseas the question of whether or not they are too apt to say that certain men are key personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am doing that continually, if I may say so.

While I am on my feet, there are two other points to which I would refer briefly. The whole question of the revision of the-points system is bound up with the army of occupation because, as I said, the ppinion appears to be- widespread among the men that a large proportion who have combat service which should entitle them to return home are being grabbed for the army of occupation.
In that connection I should like to read this extract from a letter from, a soldier overseas which bears out what I say, and which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of October 15:
The organization of the Canadian occupation force leaves much to be desired. We were both amused and disgusted to read in a Canadian newspaper that the COF was "a master-piece of administration." In reality, thousands of men were grabbed from every unit, regardless of the length of time they spent in action. No distinction was made between men who risked their all in battle and others who belatedly arrived after V-E day.
That is a situation which could be cleared up by a revision in the point system, so as to give extra credit to the men who have served in action. I was under the impression that that point had been covered. From what I have said, if anything further were necessary, I think the minister should now be convinced that there is a situation in this connection which requires clearing lip; and if he is unable, with the assistance of his staff officers, to devise some system which would cure the

situation, then I will repeat the suggestion already made, namely, that one extra point be given for every month spent in actual combat.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: And how would the hon. member define actual combat?
I am not concerned here to define that; that should be worked out by the officers on the staff.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That has been their difficulty.

If the minister wishes I will call at his office and go into the matter with him. But I suggest that surely now that we have advanced the principle, there are sufficient highly paid and capable staff officers in Canada and overseas to work it out.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They have tried.

That would merely be for repatriation from overseas, and would not apply to the discharge of those who have come back to Canada. I believe an improvement in this regard would relieve that great body of ill feeling and resentment which does exist. We are speaking of those men to whom we promised everything while they, were fighting and when we were sending them out to fight. I wonder how some of the private members on the government side feel when they know that the men overseas resent bitterly the treatment they are now getting.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: But they are not all resenting it bitterly.

How does the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) feel about it? We used to get his letters-and I am not criticizing him personally-saying how much the government was going to do for the men who were carrying the country's burdens in the field of battle. All I am saying is that we, as members of the opposition, have gone probably farther than it is necessary for us to go, but that we have suggested to the government steps which should be taken for those men who carried the country's burdens in battle, and that it is now up to the government to get on with it.

On a point of privilege, on October 16, as reported at page 1185 of Hansard, I used these words:
Even at this eleventh hour it should be revised, and some additional bonus, some preference, should be granted or some scheme devised -I care not how you work it out-for the benefit of the men who have been in actual combat and to whom the minister referred as having the hardest and longest service.
I suggest that the minister is incorrect when he says that no alternative recommendation was made.

Demobilization-Army

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I accept my hon. friend's statement. What I meant was that no one had suggested-and I shall deal with this in greater detail after eight o'clock when I explain the difficulties the staff were up against in attempting to assess what is loosely called actual combat. That has been suggested, of course. It was considered over a year ago by those who were responsible for trying to frame a policy. But the difficulties were very great in deciding what value should be given for so-called actual combat, or how one would define actual combat, or find a record of it. However, I shall discuss this in detail at eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

There are a few matters
to which I should like to call the attention of the minister, coming as I do from a soldier city, and perhaps he would make a note of them and give me a reply later.
Does a soldier lose his civilian status by enlisting? I raised this question before in the house and the minister's predecessor gave some reply to it, but I have generally found that a soldier on enlisting does lose his civilian status. He has no longer any status at all as a civilian. We have seen that in the past two years, particularly in the case of a soldier called "Tiger" Welsh, who came in for a good deal of criticism because he gave an interview to a newspaper, and the rule then was made that soldiers must not give interviews to newspapers. But the war is over now and I hope the minister will look into that question again. I believe that at the present time it is doing a great injury to the national interest.
The first-in, first-out rule is a very good rule in principle, but it has not been working out very well. I urged away back last July in an interview with the Globe that the government should follow the practice which was adopted when the war broke out of establishing a shipping pool agency in Washington. Through that agency we got a large quantity of supplies and equipment and troops and many ships on lease. The war has been over now for some months and we need shipping to bring our troops home. The government should follow the same practice and establish an agency in Washington through which we might be able to get the use of some United States ships for bringing our men home. Not long ago the Cunard line of steamships and 47696-102
other ships of British registry were filled with United States soldiers to sixty per cent of their capacity. Notwithstanding the shipping pool I believe that the government could do more to get shipping to bring our soldiers home. More trips by the Queen Elizabeth and the lie de France could be arranged for, as well as the use of Dutch boats. Repatriation has been going on a little better in the last two or three months but still there is an insistent clamour from our people to get the boys back home for Christmas, and I urge that everything be done to bring that about. We all remember what a miracle in transport was worked after Dunkirk. Another miracle should be worked to-day in demobilizing our troops faster by land, sea and air to get them home.
Another matter I wish to bring up is the cadet services. What is to be done about them? I notice that a member from the province of Quebec claimed the other day that Quebec had more cadet services than the city of Toronto, but he forgot about the 60,000 cadets in our public and secondary schools.
I should like to see the government do something about turning back to the municipalities, cities, towns and rural municipalities of this country the property which they turned over to the government for use during the war. Take the Canadian National exhibition property in Toronto, for instance; there is no reason why that property should not be given back to the city. Some of the buildings are not occupied, and in addition there are a large number of sheds along the waterfront east of Yonge street. Action is needed at once to aid housing this winter.
The trouble that I see when a new minister comes into a department is that the minute he takes hold, along comes the deputy minister and persuades him to do things like the last minister did, and the result is that the policy of the new minister is exactly the policy of the old. That is all very well in the days of peace. But in these days greater activity is needed. The new post office building on Bay street should also be given back to the post office at once by the army. All the minister needs to do is to order them to move and it will be done. The property that was turned over to the government by the municipalities for use in war time should be turned back now.
There are a lot of soldiers appearing in the courts to-day, civilian and other courts. I read the newspapers and I find that many of these soldiers have no lawyer to represent them in court. I raised this question with the minister's predecessor last year. I appreciate
Demobilization-Army

what the Canadian Bar Association has done, but I saw a letter in the Globe and Mail the other day written by Colonel Myall of Hamilton, referring to a member of the forces, a decorated man who was sent down for a trivial offence and had no lawyer to represent him in court. Something should be done about this. If private organizations do not do it, the minister should have an official of his own to appear in court on behalf of the soldier.
Industry is badly in need of reconversion. Cannot we d,o something to cut through the mass of red tape and unlock the handcuffs which prevent men from getting out of the forces, especially those who have already come back to Canada? How is industry to march forward with a scarcity of men? There must be more activity shown in demoblization to aid reconversion, and more modern methods adopted, so as to create a steady flow of civilian goods and aid industry.
I have often urged reduced railway fares for soldiers, and I had hopes that something along this line would be done, but the members of the forces are still being charged the same fares, even on week-ends. I hope something along that line will be done.
I should not like to see the government adopt the wide policy of President Truman and make all youths under twenty years of age take one year of military training. Consider what our schools in the cadet services have done already for the armed forces in two great wars. The public and separate schools did splendidly in the South African war and many wars since then, and they were the backbone of our militia in the great war, through the cadet training in the schools. The separate schools also have a splendid cadet corps, De La Salle. Also the public secondary schools of all provinces have done wonderful work for the militia in the cadet services. They have cadet instructors, camps,' rifle drill and all that sort of thing. I should not like to see a young Canadian lose a whole year from university or industry by having to take compulsory military training when he can take it at school with military drill.
'Last July an order was issued permitting high school students in the armed forces to be discharged in order that they might resume their studies at high school or the university. I see no reason why that order should not be extended to include those who are serving overseas and who left high school or their first year at university. Some of them are now in the army of occupation in Germany. All they can do under the present regulations 
is to go overseas to the Khaki college. They should be permitted to come home, the same as those in Canada, to resume their education.
Last week in reply to a question I raised, a return was tabled about deserters overseas and in Canada. Some of these deserters during the heavy fighting in Italy were away for a couple of weeks. I do not think some of them, after being over there three or four years, were in their right minds; some of them were nervous wrecks; yet some of them were sentenced to as much as five and ten years. Now, upon being returned to Canada, some of them have been removed from Fort Henry to a federal penal institution. I notice, according to a report in the Toronto Globe, that one of the Quebec members, speaking at East Brome, said that terms for deserters in his constituency were only twenty-eight days' detention, and that he got them out. Surely these matters ought to be looked into, and an inquiry held at once into these irregularities. When the navy estimates were up I was glad to observe a remark of the minister about the case of those men who got into trouble at Halifax; he seems to have taken a reasonably sensible view of the matter, and I hope that something will be done to release them without all this delay and red tape of clemency departments.
In conclusion, let me say that no city in the dominion has given more of. its property to the government for use in the war than has Toronto. I hope the minister, unlike others I have referred to, in the administration of his department will not be content to do merely as the deputy says, but will make a thorough house-cleaning, and will enable the city to get back some of its property so that it can go ahead to provide some housing for the people in the coming winter, and a start at reopening the Canadian National exhibition.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall take note of what my hon. friend has raised and try to give him an answer later. *
I should like to say a few words about matters raised this afternoon concerning the method which has been followed of repatriating our troops. If in the heat of debate I appeared to be impatient, I do not wish to convey to hon. members that I do not want to hear any suggestions which they may have. I know I am voicing the views of all members of the committee when I say that the objects of us all are the same, namely, to ensure that the system we have is the most perfect one to get our troops home as quickly as possible and in the fairest way possible. I do not want to give the impression that either I or the members of the staff have a

Demobilization-Army
rigid mind in these matters and are not open to any suggestions for improving the system. But I wish to explain to the committee, perhaps a little more fully than it has been possible to do in the past, how that system has been worked out.
The criticisms which have been made this afternoon boil down, it seems to me, to two main points. The first is that the system as arranged has permitted low-point men, including N.R.M.A. men, to return with their units ahead of men with very much higher points.
Even though they have done no fighting.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am going to deal with the second point later. That is the first point. They may or may not have done any fighting. There are some N.R.M.A. men who did fighting, and about two hundred were killed; some low-point men did considerable fighting. The point raised by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar was slightly different. He thought that low-point men who had done fighting should come home ahead of high-point men who had done no fighting. There is a difference of view there.
The second point is that the point system of repatriation should provide some weighting for men who had engaged in actual combat or who had done fighting; those were the phrases used. The hon. member for Nanaimo quoted my statement that men who had done the longest and hardest service should be brought home first, but interpreted "hardest" as meaning "most dangerous." I point out to him and the committee that the phrase is "longest and hardest," which is not necessarily "longest and most dangerous"; and the basic principle which was followed in working out this system which was adopted was that it was length of separation from those in Canada, rather than the degree of danger which may have been involved in the service performed, which governed the point system.
On a point of privilege, I never mentioned the word "dangerous."

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No; I pointed out that my hon. friend appeared to interpret my phrase "longest and hardest" in the sense that "hardest" would imply "more dangerous."
I do not know where the minister got that interpretation. It is merely his idea of how, as he thinks, I should have interpreted those words.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If I have taken the wrong
meaning from my hon. friend's language, perhaps the point is not of great importance. I will elaborate. This whole plan came under consideration by the army demobilization 47696- I02i	.
planning committee which was set up in August, 1944. They canvassed all the various elements which they felt should be taken into consideration in trying to work out a system for determining the basis on which troops should be returned from overseas. It was pretty well agreed, I think, that that system should fulfil certain requirements. First, it should be simple and easily understood; second, it should be susceptible of easy, efficient administration; third, it should be of general application and equally fair to all who were on the same basis. Finally, it should be readily calculable from existing documents and records. They considered whether some such test as combat service or fighting should be taken into consideration, and it was finally decided not to adopt any such test, for a variety of reasons, I understand, but mainly because in this war it is very difficult to define what is a battlefield, an area of combat, or combat service. May I say in parenthesis that other countries have experienced the same difficulty, and I am advised that there is no state in the commonwealth which has worked out a system whereby points are awarded for so-called combat duty. It has no,t been done in Great Britain or Australia or South Africa or New Zealand. The only country I know of which has done it is the United States. The way they have been able to do it is that apparently they awarded decorations and stars for combat duty. They have a decoration known as the Purple Heart, and they award so many points for a Purple Heart, so many points for decorations for gallantry, so many points for combat stars, and so on. Rightly or wrongly, we have not that system of decorations; but it is important to note that the records of the individual soldier do not indicate whether he has had combat service or not. I repeat that the method of keeping records does not indicate whether a man has combat service, actual combatant service, or whatever phrase one chooses to take. Obviously it would be quite possible to assess each individual soldier on an individual basis, and determine whether or not he had combatant service or one of those other types of service which, it is suggested, should give him somewhat higher points for repatriation; but our records do not indicate that, and the records of other commonwealth nations do not indicate it; the records of the United States forces apparently do, but only to the extent that a man has been awarded a ribbon or a star or a decoration for combat.

Would the minister
allow a question at this point?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes, gladly.
Demobilization-Army

Is he not aware that our records do show definitely when a man goes into a theatre of operations; it appears on his records and can be got without any difficulty in the world, and it was on the basis of those records that the original point system of which I spoke this afternoon was worked out, and points were assigned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My hon. friend is now using another phrase. He says "a theatre of operations." I know of no particular reason why a man who served, let us say, at a base in France should have a higher priority for repatriation than a man who served, say, in a depot in the dock area in London which was being bombed night after night. He is talking now about a theatre of operations.
I am glad he raised the point about the point score which was used for rotation leave. That dealt with a comparatively small number of men who could be handled on the individual basis to which I refererd a moment ago. [DOT]
I am not an expert in these matters and I do not know whether it would have been administratively possible to do it. I have to take the word of officers whom I believe to be extremely capable in matters of this kind, and if the committee stopped to think it over, I think they would realize that these officers, in common with all the rest of us, have just as much interest in seeing that a fair and equitable system of returning our lads from overseas is worked out. They are just as fair as any of the rest of us. After all, the question is one which involves the exercise of judgment, and the judgment which has been exercised in this particular matter is that of senior and not so senior officers here, overseas and in London who, I can assure the committee, after the most exhaustive and careful study, have concluded, rightly or wrongly, that this is on balance the fairest and most workable system that can be devised. And I can say to the committee that it is working fairly.
Perhaps I should give some figures with regard to the repats in the month of September. I got these figures during the recess because I thought it might be interesting to the committee to see how the system works out. In September the reduction in strength from overseas was 35,301, and this is the way in which it worked out. Those with a point score of over 150 were 21,305; those with a point score of 130 to 149-and, mark you, these are all high point men-were 3,673; those with a point score of 100 to 129 were 3,550; and from 50 to 100 there were only 7,000 out of that total. In other words,

well over three-quarters were high-point score men. That is the way in which the present system is actually working.
How many were N.R.M.A.?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I have not that figure, but I can assure my hon. friend that they were a relatively small number. Perhaps I can answer that point with regard to the N.R.M.A. A certain number of N.R.M.A. men, low-point men, were sent to units in northwest Europe and Germany up to V-E day and shortly after. But remember, cessation of hostilities on V-E day did not mean that our troops in northwest Europe and Germany were not still charged with the carrying out of extremely important responsibilities. They had to see that civil order was maintained, that towns were occupied, and that sort of thing, and you could not send completely untrained troops to replace the shortages in those battalions. As I mentioned this afternoon, reinforcements sent forward to the theatre just prior to V-E day and for a short time afterwards were sent forward in the ordinary way, taking their ordinary turn in the reinforcement queue, and there was no arrangement whereby low-point men went sent forward' in order that they might be repatriated quickly. They continued to serve in those units.
I am not going to stand here and say that the system which has been adopted is the perfect system or one which is not susceptible of improvement, but I do say that it is the system which has been worked out by men who, in my judgment at any rate, are extremely competent officers. It represents their considered view as to what is the most workable system. I have no doubt they will take into account the points brought forward in this debate, for instance.
The system is working. It is working well, and on balance-and you can only take these things on balance and on averages-I do not know that a much better system could have been evolved. From the information I have been given I can certainly say to the committee that the system of any other of our associated or allied nations i9 working no better than if as well as our own.
Nobody else has an N.R.M.A. set-up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If I may interject, the N.R.M.A. portion of this problem is a very small one. I will even, concede for the sake of argument that it is unfortunate that these low-point N.R.M.A. men were included. But one of the main points this afternoon was-I think my hon. friend the member for Nanaimo will agree with me

that we should change

Demobilization-Army
our system and give a special allocation of points to men who had had combat duty. I have endeavoured to explain that that question was considered by the officers who were studying the matter and* was discarded for the reasons which I have tried to put before the committee. I have- bolstered my point, if you like, by stating that no other country, with the exception of the United States, has been able to devise a system whereby special points can be awarded for this type of combat duty or whatever it may be, serving in an operational theatre, to use the phrase of the hon. member for Calgary East. The United States have a system of decoration different from ours which facilitates easy determination of the question as to who had this type of service.
I cannot say more to the committee. I shall bring the points which have been* raised in the course of this discussion to the attention of the staff, but I feel sure the committee will appreciate that this is not a matter which is now or which should be made the subject of political controversy. We are all anxious to see that a system is operated which will be as fair and efficient as possible.
As minister I am dependent upon the advice of officers whom I believe to be extremely competent in matters of this kind and I certainly would not attempt to substitute my judgment for theirs on such questions. They certainly have as great an interest as I have in seeing that the system works smoothly and I hope they are open to suggestions. But I assure the committee that they have given this particular problem the most serious consideration and after that consideration have decided* that the, system which we have adopted is probably the most workable one, taking into account all the circumstances. I do not think there is anything more I can add to that statement.

One question about the United States system. I understand that any soldier who has seen two campaigns is automatically discharged. Is that not so? Could we not determine how many soldiers had seen two campaigns? How many have we left in Europe who have seen two campaigns? According to the United States system, I understand that if a man served in Africa and Italy he is discharged automatically, and the same is true if he served in Italy and western Europe. Could we not find out the facts, in regard to such service so far as we are concerned? We have records.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Our people have studied closely the plans of all other allied and associated countries, and I have here a booklet
which I have been given as outlining the United States system, but it does not indicate that special consideraiton is given to a case such as my hon. friend has mentioned, though that may well be possible. May I say, without casting reflections on the United States system, that reports reaching me indicate that there is, if I may put it in the form of understatement, no greater satisfaction with the United States system of repatriation than there is with ours. I have heard of cases of the system resulting in a thousand men being left under a subaltern, which any old soldier realizes is not an entirely satisfactory way of running either an army of occupation or a number of men left for repatriation.
I do not want to be dogmatic. Both I and the officers are quite open to suggestions and I am glad that we have had this discussion to-day. But it is very easy to say that we should award special points for combat duty. It appeals to all of us; we all feel that it should be done. When one gets down to the practical realities, however, and, in the handling of 150.000, 175,000, or 200,000 men, tries to make ..use of available shipping, so that a ship will not sail with empty space that might accommodate a thousand men who could be brought back to Canada, it is not so simple as it seems.
This system has been pretty carefully thought out. I am assured it has been and I believe that to be the case. It is perhaps subject to some further improvement; but in my judgment, for what it is worth, we cannot now substitute a system of trying to give some credits for combat duty or serving in an operational theatre when our thousands of records do not contain a definite indication as to what man is entitled to it. By the time we started to make that arrangement it would be the middle or the end of December, and we hope we shall have a lot more men back before that time. I have pointed out to the committee the way in which the point system is working, and incidentally I might, point out that the basis of computing points terminated on March 31, 1945, so that there is no question of accumulating further points* for service overseas after March 31, 1945.
The system shows that over three-quarters* of those who came back in September were men with 150 points or better. Naturally, with points frozen on March 31, 1945, the point score of the average man overseas is* going steadily down. I shall bring every suggestion that has been made to the attention of the officers who are responsible for working -out this plan; but I can sincerely say to the-committee, I do think the plan is working: well and frankly I deprecate too much dis

Demobilization-Army

cussion which may tend to create further doubts in the minds of the men overseas as to the fairness of the system. I, myself, do not believe that it is unfair and I hope that the men overseas are not getting that impression.
Incidentally, a certain number of statements have been made here this afternoon to the effect that men coming back from overseas are resentful of the system, and feel that it is unfair. Well, some may feel that, but I have been in 'touch with as many as I could, friends of mine have been coming back and quite frankly that is not the impression I have got from them. Some of them have said, just as has been said here this afternoon, that some consideration should be given to men who have had fighting service; but when I have explained the difficulties of that to them, they have said, "Well, I guess perhaps that is right, and' it is working pretty well too." I am satisfied that we are doing the best we can. Really, there is nothing more I can add to that statement?
The minister made several points. He deprecated the introduction of politics into this question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No; I said there were no politics in it.
I wanted to assure myself on that point, because there certainly is not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I made it clear that I was sure nobody was speaking on this from a political point of view.

Most certainly not. The minister has made a very interesting statement, but he has not answered the questions we raised this afternoon, namely, that there should be additional points awarded for each month of what we call fighting service, or combat service. It was not until the minister himself suggested that there was any difficulty in deciding what was combat service that it ever crossed my mind that there could be any difficulty on that score at all, and after hearing him I still think there is no difficulty.
The position we are taking is the position taken by a great number of soldiers. I have a clipping here which simply says: "Main objection to the point system was that it gives no extra credit for combat service," and that the troops returning were resentful. In sny opinion, and I think in the opinion of *jvery Canadian soldier, the test of comlbat ervice is this: Do you wear the Africa star? Jo you wear the Italy star, or do you wear the northwest Europe star? That is the test of fighting service which entitles a man to a campaign ribbon of .which he may well be proud. Whether he is a cook, or wherever he [Mr. Abbott.!
is in the theatre of operations he is what I call a fighting soldier, and that system would suit me perfectly well. Therefore the plan proposed by the members on this side of the house is this: one extra point for every month of service which entitles you to a campaign ribbon. Therefore it is very simple. Perhaps the minister will say that it is too simple, but it would suit the fighting soldiers.
The other point that I think we made was that the system should be revised now. I should like the minister to say whether or not since the articles came out in the Maple Leaf, and since it was apparent that there was dissatisfaction with the present system, he has on his own initiative asked General Simmonds, or any other of the high ranking officers on whom he relies, if some change along the lines that we have suggested, which would still the dissatisfaction that the men have expressed, could be made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I can answer that question very quickly. I did take it up, and I have a long and very full memorandum from General Simmonds in which he strongly recommends that no change ibe made in the present system. I received that memorandum about a week or ten days ago.

I
should like to shift the emphasis a little into the future. We assume that the estimates which have been presented to us are in line with our commitments or possible commitments to the united nations. Obviously we cannot defend ourselves alone. Our best hope of defence is in cooperation with other countries collectively; and yet I think it is equally obvious that we may not be able to defend ourselves at all with armies and with navies. We may hope that we can control technology, but that is merely a protestation of faith. Faith without good works is not of very much use to us.
On August. 6 our entire conception of military strategy was revolutionized. We then found out that armies could be wiped out and navies obliterated, because the scientist and the technician are now supreme.
The basic principles of strategy by which we fought for two thousand years went up in the smoke of Hiroshima, and I think not only our armies but our navies also are perhaps outmoded. The same may also be true of our air force. We are told that the atomic bomb is an experiment. Well, it was quite an experiment, if what we are told is true, that two hundred of those bombs have the power of devastation of two million tons of bombs such as we have known before. I say that our air force may be outmoded because the bomb

Demobilization-Army
may conceivably be used as a rocket projectile ; and as the months and perhaps the years go by, greater skill will be foundi to direct that projectile with much greater accuracy. Obviously then to-day as far as defence goes we are in the hands of the scientist, and I should like to know what the minister is doing in this field. What is being done by the Department of National Defence to encourage the scientist? From the point of view of defence I think it would be a better investment to have two thousand scientists employed than ten times that number of men in the armed forces. What is being done to keep these men in Canada and to use them for the defence of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I have already dealt with
the matter. In my opening statement I dealt to some extent with the steps which were being taken to encourage research and development. I dealt, I think, also at some length in replies to a number of questions asked by the hon. member for Nanaimo the other day. I indicated that the three different services have now under active consideration-when I say "active consideration" I really mean it-just how the research and development activities of the three'services can be most actively and efficiently carried on, and carried on in the closest cooperation with the national research council. I indicated that I hoped in the not too far distant future to be able to make a more definite statement as to just what plans had been worked out, but I assure the committee that this very important phase of defence activities is not being overlooked.

I am not prepared to depart from the discussion of the point system at the moment, because I believe sufficient evidence has been produced to show there is widespread dissatisfaction with the way in which men are being repatriated from overseas. I have every confidence, as I believe every hon. member has confidence, in our commanders overseas; but when this point system was first prepared those commanders were busily engaged in battle or had just finished the operations which brought victory. They were concerned with the immediate problems which faced them on the continent of Europe. I feel sure there must have been some connection maintained between the department here and those commanders overseas. Staff officers were crossing to Europe quite frequently, and no doubt they discussed the repatriation system. I do not think it is quite fair to unload the burden upon General Crerar and General [DOT]Simmonds and suggest that they were entirely responsible for preparing the present point .system.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It was not prepared here in Canada.

I did not say, here in
Canada. I said that Canadian staff officers made frequent visits to England. Nt>
doubt those officers did discuss this problem with General Crerar and General Simmonds, but those two officers were concerned with immediate operations. However, no general officer is infallible, and now we have had six months of experience with the working out of this point system. The very figures which were given us to-day, indicating that some seven thousand low-point men had been brought back in one month; the press reports which have been read to us from various newspapers in Canada, emphasize the fact that the present system is not working satisfactorily. Those press reports did not come from Saskatchewan only. The minister referred to the Saskatoon Light Infantry, but other units came back at that time and all but two included a proportion of more than ten per cent of low-point men, according to a return tabled here a couple of weeks ago. It has been admitted already that the minister has received a number of letters in this connnection, some of them passed on by members of parliament. I know I have had many letters, a few of which I have passed on to the minister. They all report a feeling of dissatis-tion abroad that the men who have seen the longest and hardest service are not coming back first. I should like to read an extract from one letter I received:
Some of your remarks came very close home to us.
That is in reference to some remarks I made here in the house.
We have a boy who is planted, I consider, quite unfairly in the army of occupation. I have tried every w'ay I know of, except political pressure, to get him repatriated to Canada to pursue a medical course at McGill university before he becomes too old. All I ha've got out of the adjutant general is the statement of policy in regard to occupational service, and the bemoaning of the fact that his case typifies one of their greatest problems.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend know
the point score of that soldier?

I do not know the point
score, but I am coming to his service in a moment:
Their greatest problem started with the injustice of the point system which, you have properly pointed out.	.
Our boy landed on the beaches of Normandy on D-day with the 19th Field Regiment, R.C.A., and his unit was through the thick of it until V-E day almost without a break, yet he does not rate consideration. . . .
Here is a young man who landed on the beaches on D-day, so I am told-
Demobilization-Army

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
He might have a point
score of only sixty.
He is anxious to come back and take a university course, but he cannot come back. That is only one example. I do not know his point score.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It is of some importance.

That information was not given me, but it can be ascertained. If it is a high-point score he should be permitted to come back, but this is a typical example of what may be found all over Canada. It is not only in one province; it is.in every province throughout the country. I say sufficient evidence has been produced to show that this point system, as it is in operation at the present time, is working to the disadvantage of the man who has seen the longest and hardest service. Therefore I ask, is it not possible now for the minister to consider revising that point system on some such simple plan as was just suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, under which a man who is entitled to wear a service ribbon would get a bonus.
I should like to make a few observations with respect to the estimates generally.
I wonder if I might just put one question on this same subject.

I will not be too long. To-day I checked over the defence estimates for the last year of the Conservative regime in this country, 1935-36, and I.was interested to note that the figure approximated $17,000,000. During the first year war was declared the Liberal government budgeted for an expenditure of $65,000,000. Last year the estimates reached the comparatively astronomical figure of $1,500 million for the army alone. In other words, the army estimates for the year just past are approximately nine hundred times what they were when we were standing by with our head in the sand, so to speak, thinking all was well with the world.
Thanks to Miss Macphail.

She may have had something to do with it; however, a number of Conservatives had the same ideas at the same time. We have made terrific war expenditures, and-now in the first year of peace we are going to spend for the army alone roughly a billion dollars, if these estimates pass as I believe they will.

It is with respect to some personal criticisms, that I am on my feet now. When our spending was very niggardly in regard to defence we had what might be called an emaciated staff, but when we got into the war and as the war proceeded that was changed. District depots; district headquarters; the Department of National Defence; Canadian military headquarters; the first and second echelons of twenty-one army group; the headquarters of the first Canadian army; the headquarters of two corps; the headquarters of five divisions, with all their entourage

all these were created one after another and gradually expanded until now we have reached what I think could well be called a state of administrative obesity. We are going to have about as much trouble in reducing that staff to sensible proportions in the next year or two as a fat man would have in taking off the generous amounts of lard he may have accumulated during better days.
A few days ago I drew attention to the amount of brass hanging around Ottawa, and this evening I should like to make a correction in the statement I made at that time. On that occasion I said that on V-E day there were 1,582 army officers at Ottawa; I have found that actually there were somewhere between 1,677 and 1,933 officers at national defence headquarters. Then, in London, at C.M.H.Q. we have actually increased since January 1 the number of officers from 478 to 526. There is, of course, a small sprinkling of other rank personnel as well. For example, in Ottawa on the last day of September there were about 5,500 other ranks, while in London at C.M.H.Q. there were about 2,300. In other words, in those two headquarters groups alone we have an officer complement

and with plenty of extras, particularly at the higher levels-for seven fighting divisions, and we have half a division of other ranks. Those are the proportions.
I have no doubt that in spite of the unwieldy strength of these establishment they did assist materially in the successful conclusion of the war, so far as Canada is concerned. It is a moot question, of course, as to whether we could have had as successful results with fewer staff officers.	,
There has been a phenomenal improvement in our fighting equipment. I can recall the early days of the war when in our artillery batteries we did gun drill with broomsticks, because of a lack of actual guns. Ultimately, of course, we got those excellent 25-pounders which did such effective work against the enemy. That is, after a very considerable period1 of time we managed to secure the type of equipment which was actually necessary for

Demobilization-Army
the successful prosecution, of the war. But I believe that these expenditures in terms of actual equipment used, which will now be scrapped, are far in excess of our expenditures for the personal welfare of the troops who manipulated that expensive equipment.
We had overseas two groups of services which catered especially to the well-being of the man. I refer to the Canadian auxiliary services and to the Canadian Legion educational services. I think this would be a proper time to pay tribute to what was done by them. The first group I have mentioned in connection with their canteen and entertainment work. This was done at a time when it was badly needed. I would refer, too, to the work of the Canadian Legion educational services, and their successors the Canadian army educational services, which filled a need felt by the men when they were not particularly interested in entertainment. Special tribute is due to the staff of the Canadian army educational services for the excellent work they did in the lines, behind the lines and at bases, and for what they are now doing at khaki college in England.
In this connection, however, I should like to read briefly from an excerpt from Canada's Weekly of October 5, 1945, which would seem to indicate that, in spite of our expenditures amounting to billions of dollars, it is still equipment upon which we spend our money, and not men. This article deals with the various branches of khaki college set up in London. Some hon. members may know the place in Watford where No. 10 hospital was located. We have, through the khaki college, set up facilities which cater to about 193 persons who are taking advanced university training, and 576 who are taking other university and vocational type courses. This is a branch- of the Canadian army educational services, set up in cooperation with Dr. Chatwin, Director of Canadian Legion educational services, which is now under the command of Brigadier Beament, of Ottawa.
However, one would think that, now that the war is over, these boys have earned this education at the hands of a grateful people, and that they should get it free of charge, too. I quote the following:
In the first instance a large number of applications for attendance at the various universities have been withdrawn after the prospective student has received an estimate or the cost of living and the fee payable on entrance.
I am referring to service students.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Where are these men, here or overseas?
Overseas, in khaki college.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
They are not charged
anything.

The article continues:
Many have found it utterly impossible to meet these expenses on their present army pay and allowances-particularly N.C.O.'s and other ranks.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is no charge made at khaki college to service men.

I have quoted from a semiofficial publication, Canada's Weekly of October 5. Where a veteran wishes to take training up to and including second degree arts or science, this is provided by the junior college, and is administered by service personnel, as well as by some who have recently left Canada to assist in instruction. They are, however, required to pay a fee for attendance at the senior courses at approved English universities.
If our veterans are anxious to make use of their waiting time until they are brought home, then it seems to me that the minister should make it his duty to investigate the facts set out in this article, because I believe it states the truth. I have not quoted it to embarrass the minister, but rather to draw to his attention what I believe to be a grievous injustice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Just to have it straight, I am assured by the deputy minister that there is no charge made at khaki college for instruction.
At the junior college.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There may be a charge for a course outside the college, but not at the college itself.

Courses in third and fourth year arts or science, or post-graduate work, are not provided in the junior college; by arrangement they must be sent to London, Edinburgh, Aberystwith and so on. Our army staff or the Department of National Defence ' has not made what I think is a sane provision for their studies by way of paying for its cost at the higher levels of study.
During the period before the khaki college was set up, a large number of the boys and girls in the services were taking studies through the Canadian Legion courses or through instruction provided at regimental or unit headquarters. The administrative person for that work at regimental level was an N.C.O., a corporal, if you please. I recall that at the time I was overseas a considerable effort was made to give to that important person who was arranging these courses and even giving instruction himself in a variety of subjects, some remuneration in addition to
Demobilization-Army

the twenty cents a day which he would receive as a corporal. Yet that feature of our work overseas was so badly ignored that this instructor was put in a lower pay category than a class C clerk. In spite of that inadequate recognition of the persons who were to administer this intellectual uplifting movement, the persons charged with it worked, as I said here a few days ago, from the usual teacher's love of his work rather than because of any adequate compensation.
We used to receive glowing accounts overseas from our families of the self-sacrifice to which they subjected themselves in the way of reduced rations and the shortage of certain luxury foods so that we might have the most luscious bacon, the finest eggs, and so forth, while we were on service. During all my period overseas, I can remember nothing' in the way of bacon except the fattest of the fat. Brussel sprouts and mutton were our constant diet. In the first week or two overseas there was.no objection to that particular diet. I enjoyed the food for a few meals. But there was never an attempt made by those in charge of our rations to vary the diet or make it interesting, and when I think of that lean bacon which disappeared somewhere from Canada in order to feed us, that fat bacon which we used to have over there makes me weep. Eggs for breakfast! We had a sort of concoction that was supposed to be powdered eggs. It was made by some firm in Canada. The whites were removed. Once a month we got an egg, and on the eggs that we did receive was stamped "Product of Argentina".

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: You look pretty well and fat on it.
I am doing not too badly. But have you seen a prisoner of war six weeks after he was liberated?
Most of us got eggs only once a year.

Perhaps we were fortunate. The point was there was no equality of treatment as between the services, or as between various nationals. The air force, for example, received fruit juices in their diet, and of course the reason given, which was quite adequate so far as we were concerned, was that this supplement of fruit juices was necessary for operational flying. But when the ground crew received it too, and when the United States troops received their fruit juices, sometimes we just queried the wisdom of those senior officials who dictated that we should live on brussells sprouts and old mutton.

A lengthy discussion has taken place over the point system of repatriation. . I feel that the point system, even as it was first laid down, was quite a fair system for repatriating our boys to Canada. On paper it was a wonderful scheme. In actual practice, however, somewhere the staff work fell down. I have a very simple suggestion and, I think, a workable one. I would be willing to grant additional points for wounds or for those who had seen service in a theatre of operation. In spite of the fact that the system of two points per month for service overseas and one point per month for service in Canada never worked perfectly, it would have been a simple matter -it was being done daily in connection with every other phase of our training-when a regiment or division or brigade was slated for return to Canada to repost the low-point men from the brigade or the division to some other unit that was not slated to return and to fill up the ranks with high-point personnel from the next group due to come back. That should present no administrative problem. It could have been handled very easily. But what happened was, it was found the simplest matter to move the whole regiment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend will realize that if we had followed his suggestion through to its logical conclusion we would have ended up entirely with men with fifty points or less staying overseas. All your administrative officers and your N.C.O.s would have come back.

I agree with that in all its details, except for this, that you still would have had quite a number of administrative officers and N.C.O.s who would have been quite anxious to remain on the other side of the water for some time, so that it would have been possible to allocate from among them the officers and N.C.O.'s required for administrative work overseas.
We also have an army or part of an army of occupation overseas. We have quite a number of officers on this side of the water.
I have just referred to 1,933 officers on the strength of the N.D.H.Q. on January 1, 1945.
I am sure that some of these officers would have been glad to go over to the continent for a couple of months, and they could have gone over in the empty boats returning to pick up other personnel.
I wish to suggest something further to the minister. I have always congratulated the government on the general framework of the discharge and rehabilitation legislation. It is good in principle but there are weaknesses, and if there are weaknesses they are in the staff

Demobilization-Army
work or administration. I believe that a system of gratuity payments, for example, should be something that is inflexible. The other evening the minister told us in this house that .an officer who had returned from overseas *duty to resume a civilian job received on April 19 of this year thirty days pay in lieu of his leave, because he was going to take an important appointment in the United States and by taking his leave he might have missed out in that appointment. I think that is the logical way to handle that thirty days repatriation leave. But that law should be inflexible, and, if necessary, retroactive to include all persons who have not received their thirty days repatriation leave, and no cut-off date of April 19, 1945, should be made because stronger representation, was made on behalf of that person instead of someone who was less insistent two months earlier.
I have received a number of communications, as have most other members of this house, with respect to applications to War Assets Corporation for materials such as trucks, farm equipment, or other things which could be turned to use in reestablishing the veteran in business of some sort. First of all, it is grossly unfair that a veteran should wait an extensive length of time to receive this surplus equipment, which is going for a song or, as has been admitted here, in many cases is being destroyed; and second, it is unfair that he should have to pay a twenty per cent dealer's commission for getting war assets material which has already been paid for.
