The minister should use his good office as a member of the cabinet-because it does concern our discharged personnel, even though they have already passed out of his hands-to make it possible for these veterans to get quick and cheap service from War Assets Corporation.
I have indicated a number of ways in which the expenditure of the moneys being asked for by the present administration could be either reduced or more wisely applied. I .should1 like to have special consideration of the two matters I have mentioned: first, rebate of educational fees in the case of the service men who are studying in Great Britain at the .present time; and, second, some quick access to War Assets Corporation on discharge for the implements which they may be able to use for their reestablishment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have taken note of my hon. friend's points and I will see that they are given consideration.

It is unfortunate that a general speech should intervene 'when we are dealing with a specific subject
of great importance to service people all over the country. I have one matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. I recognize that most of the complaints with respect to repatriation and discharge arise from those who are still overseas or have been overseas, but I wish to point out that all these complaints do not come from those overseas; some are from those who are already in Canada.
I have them from persons in the air force, in the navy and in the army, men who through long service have earned their right to discharge, I have several letters on my desk, but I have one telegram which! am going to read that reached me yesterday. I will not mention the name, but it expresses the position *of a great many already in Canada:
Opportunity laundry business Pictou. Immediate discharge army necessary. Ordnance clerk class "C" clerks frozen. 178 points, four years overseas. Your assistance requested with department to obtain my discharge.
That is typical of a great many cases I have.
I am not making any complaint against the minister; he has been very courteous and considerate toward me and so have all his officials. But the fact remains that many pressing claims such as this do not get the consideration to which they are entitled, which they have earned through long years of service. For the life of me I cannot see why a man with 178 points-we have been discussing to-day the cases of men with 100 and 75 and 50 points-and also with four years overseas should still be frozen in the armed services and not permitted to take up a business which is open to him and by which he can reestablish himself in civilian life.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That sounds just like the
sort of case which I said earlier to-day I should like personally to look into, and get the reasons. It is true that certain types of personnel-I am not now speaking of officers- are "frozen," if I may use that term. The figures I have before me at the moment cover two categories, clerks and cooks, and the case to which my hon. friend has just referred would be that of a clerk. The figures which I am given are these, that a total of 662 in that category aTe frozen, 260 with point scores below 130, and 402 with point scores over 130. Of cooks, there are 127 below 130 and 339 above 130 points. I would have to be shown fairly strong reasons, I think, why a man having 178 point who is a clerk should not be put on a Canada draft and sent home at an early day.

He is in
Canada now, in Halifax.
Demobilization-Army

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be very glad to look into that case. It is hard to understand, because he has a very high-point score, one which, if he were overseas, would entitle him to immediate repatriation unless he were performing extremely essential service. It may be one of those exceptional cases which tend to throw a bit of discredit on the system, but I find it hard to understand, and it is the kind of case that I should like to look into. The committee will, however, see from the figures I have mentioned that that is far from the general rule. There are certain types of occupation in whidh, in order to assure the smooth and speedy and efficient demobilization of the others, we have to keep a certain number of men; but I am told that they are all reviewed frequently; there is no question of pressure or special interest, and I shall be very glad to have such cases brought to my attention or the attention of any official of my department in order that they may be looked into.

I should like to say something to the minister before he goes any farther, because I seem to have the happy knack of getting out of order. I wish to ask him about the women's army. Nobody seems to mention them. They filled a very useful part in the beginning of the war and did good service. On what system are they to be discharged?	They come along and work for
four-fifths of a man's wages and do a man's job. I understand that the married women have now been allowed to leave the service, but I should like the minister in a few words to tell us what scheme is at present in operation whereby these young women who come back to civilian life can be provided for. Are they to be kept on as drivers, cooks, or stenographers? Can we have a clear-cut statement? These girls were all volunteers, every-Dne of them, and they are entitled to know vhat their future will be.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Up to the present any
member of the C.W.A.C. who asks for discharge will be granted it. We are reducing the C.W.A.C. as rapidly as possible, but the committee will realize that there is much work to be done in connection with demobilization. The corps has done splendid work during the war. The members of that body have been extremely useful in that type of work, and we are anxious to keep a considerable number until the demobilization process is completed. There is no difficulty in any member of the Canadian Army Women's Corps obtaining a discharge promptly if she so desires.

In view of the complaints that have been stated here, coming from all parts of the country, would it not

be possible to set up a section of the department to handle such complaints, to look into all cases, and if they need immediate attention to see that action is taken? I know of two cases, two sergeants who saw three and a half years' service overseas. I wrote to the department with reference to these men and received in reply two different forms of instructions as to how they were to be returned to Canada. Not believing that the information given me was correct, I -wrote again to the department, and it was agreed that the instructions I had received in the first place were wrong. As "a matter of fact, my surmise was correct. I suggest that there should be a simplification of all such matters. It would be simpler if we knew of some definite official to -whom we could write on matters pertaining to men, for their return to civilian life, who have had long service both in Canada and [DOT] overseas and whose officers may be making some mistake in connection with their discharge. Something should be done to see that justice is done by these men. I know of one man at Camp Borden who was three years overseas and was serving in the quartermaster's stores. His commanding officer stated that he was indispensable and could not get out to try to help his father who is trying to run an implement business in Barrie, Ontario, with insufficient help. The'commanding officer told this man he could not get his discharge; -he was indispensable in quartermaster's stores and could not get out until the latter part of November. Fortunately, his case was considered and he got his discharge. Such cases are coming up every day. We are receiving complaints constantly. There must be general inefficiency all along the line or we would not have these com- _ plaints, and I suggest that something be done about it. These soldiers as well as their parents and their wives are relying on members' of parliament 'to make representations on their behalf, and when we bring these cases before the government they should take some action. I suggest that something more should be done in this matter than has so far been the case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall be glad to give that request consideration. My office is receiving complaints and requests for information at the rate of a thousand a day. The department has tried to set up as efficient an organization as possible for handling complaints, and any complaint addressed to my office, if I do not see it, will be routed through the proper channels. The same will be done if complaints are addressed to the deputy minister or the secretary of the department. I

Demobilization-Army
*will consider the question raised by my hon. friend as to whether we might improve the organization for dealing more promptly with such complaints. Some hon. member this afternoon pointed out that there is a marked tendency on the part of the individual commanding officer to say, "I have an efficient man and he is indispensable", and that attitude calls for review and examination either by himself or by his superior officer. We are trying to have that done.

This commanding officer
made the statement that this particular man at Camp Borden was indispensable. I am acquainted with Camp Borden and I say that the commanding officer did not know what he was talking about.

In connection with the naval estimates I raised a question regarding . the ratio of medical officers to navy personnel, and I should like to raise the same question in connection with these estimates. In the report of the national health survey brought down some time ago the statement appears at page 185 that medical officers in all services found their work less interesting and more onerous than they had been accustomed to in civil practice. In the short time at the disposal of the committee it was not possible to study the subject exhaustively and they did not feel competent to make an arbitrary recommendation, but the ratio suggested is 3-5 to 3-7 per thousand as sufficient for medical needs. The minister mentioned six per thousand in the navy. Can he indicate when we may expect any considerable number of medical personnel to be released? If in my constituency we had a similar ratio, we would have 344 doctors serving our population, whereas we have only ten. Then men from all the services are now returning to civilian life, and they find a striking contrast between the services they had in the armed forces and those available in the different communities.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I must apologize to my hon. friend. He indicated on the naval estimates that he would ask this question in respect of the army and I asked for the information but omitted to have it to-night. I will give it under one of the items when we are considering personnel.
I understand the minister to say that the repatriation point system in operation at present was decided on in August, 1944.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No. It was not decided in August, 1944, but first came up for active consideration, according to the memorandum
furnished me. This committee to consider it was set up in August, 1944, and the matter was under consideration from that time on.
When was it finally decided?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It was finally decided
shortly after V-E day. The policy was announced after victory, which I showed to the house about May 10, 1945.

The minister said it was decided at that time that combat service should not be taken into consideration and one of the great reasons for that was that there would be a tremendous amount of administrative difficulty. The only repatriation scheme which had been in operation up to that time was the thirty-day leave scheme, and I suggest that very little administrative difficulty was experienced in the working of that scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Because the numbers were so small. We were dealing with a relatively small number of men on an individual basis.

There was no more difficulty in determining what a man's point score was under the scheme used for the thirty-day plan than there would be in determining his point score under the present system. His record had to be looked into just the same to see what time he went overseas so that his points could be worked out. I still fail to see how administrative difficulty can be successfully pleaded as an excuse or a reason for the present system. One of the other points the minister made was that when the scheme was being considered the separation of a man from his family in Canada should be one of the main considerations or criteria as to when he would return. That is one of the very things I object to in the present scheme. Men who went overseas and had up to a year's actual fighting service and are still there are not being returned, whereas men who did not get into the fighting at all and spent three or four months overseas have been returned. In other words, one of the principal criteria as laid down by the minister himself is not being followed.
There is one other point I would comment upon. The minister says this system is fair. I made it a point, particularly when I was at home, of going down to meet the trains coming in and bringing back men from overseas. Since I have been here, the battery which I commanded, the 51st from Ottawa, has arrived back home, and I have seen a large number of men who served in that battery. I can tell
Demobilization-Army

the minister that I have not yet found a single man among all those men who thinks that the system in use at the present time is fair.

I do not know just how seriously the minister is taking the suggestions that we are making on this side of the house, but we are in deadly earnest on the question as to whether or not the system of repatriation is fair to the men who did the fighting.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: So am I.

We do not believe that it is fair and we believe that it can be improved. We demand that improvements be made. It is not good enough for the minister to come into the house and hide behind his officers.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am not hiding behind anybody. I have stated my case and I have told the reasons.
I repeat that it is not good enough for the minister to hide behind his officers overseas and the officers in Canada. It is not good enough for him to say that he deprecates any discussion on this.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I did not say I deprecated any discussion. Please quote me accurately.
Yes, you did. The minister said it might make trouble overseas and he deprecated having this question discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I said no such thing.
A stand which he had no right to take.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: He has denied it.
You keep out of this for a minute.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Observe the rules of decency and order.
You will have enough to do to look after your own business.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have no trouble.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Hon. members will kindly address the Chair.
Hear, hear.
I repeat that we are very much concerned about the repatriation policy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: You have no monopoly on that.

Just wait a minute. We are concerned particularly about the way in which it will work a few months hence when you come to deal with the boys who are now in the army of occupation. We believe that the
[Mr. Harkness.}
men in the army of occupation who have done-the fighting should have a chance to get home-at the first possible opportunity. Take, for example, the case of a boy who was wounded and had not been overseas very long. Last year men were sent over from this country half trained. They were rushed into action before they should have been. Perhaps they were in action only three or four months, were wounded and put back into action again. These are the young lads who are being treated unfairly by the policy of the present government, and I think the whole thing goes back to the man-power policy of the government, to a refusal right up to this very minute to recognize the fact that there were some men who volunteered to fight and die for Canada, and there were some men who did not. We have overseas N.R.M.A. troops who were forced to go over. It has been admitted by the government that some of these men who did not get to France, did not get to the continent until after the fighting had stopped, have come home in the first division. There is no fairness in that. You cannot make that fair if you argued here for ten years. The picture is so clearly put by a young lad who-wrote to me on behalf of his company from the army of occupation that I feel I should read the letter. He said that he had not been in action for very many months, but he had been in action and he is now stuck in the army of occupation. This is what he said:
Most of us in this occupational army are low-point men, but we have spent more time in northwest Europe (Holland and Germany), than we did taking training in Canada. We are all entitled to wear our C.V.S.M, and clasp, or does that ribbon mean anything any more? Along with that ribbon many of us wear "action" ribbons. We have seen four, five, six or more months of action, which is a lot for an infantryman.
And those of us who were in the infantry in the last war know how true that is.
Yet we lack the points to go home. Our main idea during the war was to get it all over with as soon as possible, so that we could return to our loved ones in Canada. That was our uppermost thought in action, yet now we are stuck up here doing occupation (we certainly didn't volunteer for it), and hear reports of N.R.M.A. personnel, who came overseas as late as June, who are now going home with the first and second divisions. They all earned their points by sitting in Canada in safety. Was it them that we fought for and are now doing occupation for, so they could march home with the regiments we fought in? They are the ones that will no doubt be claimed as the heroes by the people of Canada.
None of us want to be claimed as heroes. All we want to see is fair play. We went active to fight a war for them. Why can't they do our occupation for us? What are all the remaining N.R.M.A. (there must be thousands of them) personnel doing in Canada now?

Demobilization-Army
No doubt living off the fat of the land and wondering how soon it will be before they get their discharge. If they did not want to fight for their country, they can at least come over now and represent Canada in the occupational force, since all the danger of war has been eliminated now. Let a few of our young veterans (for anyone who sees action is a veteran) return back to Canada and help make a name for themselves in peace time Canada. We fought, and a great many of our friends who came overseas with us last year, died for Canada. Now are we to sweat it out over here while waiting for the N.R.M.A. to get out of the army?
The editor of the Maple Leaf, our overseas newspaper, Major MacFarlane, was dismissed from his post for upholding the rights of the fighting man in his editorials. If there were more men like him defending the active soldiers wc might get a break.
What is the position? A man who is wounded gets no points despite the fact that he is wounded. The minister said they could not tell who had been in action, that it was impossible to find that out. He knows or should know that every infantry man-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I did not say it was impossible.

-has been in action and is entitled to consideration for being in action.
With regard to the N.R.M.A. personnel, let us get down to a few figures about the situa-tipn. According to a return tabled, as appears at page 603 of Hansard the army of occupation consisted of 1,177 officers and 19,088 other ranks on September 1, 1945, a total of slightly over 20,000. Of that number 594 officers and 5,489 other ranks have volunteered for the army of occupation. That is over 6,000 of the 19,000, which leaves about 13,000 who must be taken into consideration. The minister should tell us how many N.R.M.A. troops there are in Great Britain. He should tell us whether or not the second division is going to come home with its units partly filled with N.R.M.A. troops who have never been in action, and the third division, and the fifth division and the fourth division. He should tell us whether the government is going to continue to fail to recognize the difference between a man who was willing to fight for his country and one who was not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have already dealt with that. So far as I am concerned, there are not two armies overseas. When they get over there, there is no distinction.

You have two here in
Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have referred to them as well.

You should have the same
policy in both places. In Canada what have
you? The answer is found on page 586 of Hansard. As of August 15, 1945, there were 35,950 N.R.M.A. troops in Canada, of whom 8,235 were out on extended leave, in otheT words, were out taking jobs to which somebody from overseas was entitled; 26,321 were still actively engaged in the N.R.M.A. army in Canada, and 1,394 in adjacent territories.
Last April the minister told me there were about 20,000 trained N.R.M.A. men who could be sent overseas as infantry at that time. Surely there is no fairness in not using these men to fill up the army of occupation and let the men who have been in action come back. We want the government to give us the figures about these N.R.M.A. troops; they enter into the picture very decidedly. We cannot reach a proper policy unless they are taken into consideration; and we believe, I repeat, there can be no fairness about this thing at all unless these men are used in the army of occupation to replace those young Canadians who have faced the enemy in action.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 1 carry?
No.

I offer no apologies, Mr. Chairman, for rising to take part in this discussion a second time this evening. I wish to associate myself most wholeheartedly with what has just been said by the hon. member for Vancouver South, and to say how much more I feel 'as I felt sometimes when we were overseas, that it is nice to know there are one or two individuals in this House of Commons who had the interests of the men overseas at heart-
Oh, oh.
-and who would not be howled down, as an attempt was made to do to-night when they rose to speak about them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
One or two men in this
house with the interests of the overseas men at heart!
Yes, and I repeat that. If the minister truly had the interests of those men at heart he would not have made the statement he did make almost immediately after the committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I can assure my young
friend that I have the interests of the men overseas at heart just as much as he has.

I realize that one speaking
as I am to-night is in a somewhat difficult position, but I make no apology for that statement because in effect the minister has admitted that the point system as at present carried out does prejudice the man who has
Demobilization-Army

seen action overseas. Yet in effect he says he is not going to change that system because that would be too difficult. That is what I had in mind when I spoke as I did. I know everyone wants to serve the men overseas and look after their interests; but difficulties are put in the way which we say should not be allowed to enter the picture for a moment or to prejudice the chances of arriving at a fair solution. That was what I meant when I made the statement I did make. I am not going to have it taken, as apparently is being attempted, that I am standing up here saying that we are the only ones who have the interests of the men overseas at heart, that no one else is at all interested. But I do say we are concerned about forcing a definite decision on this issue, as to whether or not the point system for repatriation from overseas will be changed. That is why I say I offer no apologies for taking part in this discussion a second time at this stage.
I am also anxious to. say a word, because I want to point out that the minister, in indicating the basis adopted in arriving at the present point system, stated that the main consideration was the greatest length of separation from those in Canada and not the most dangerous service. I want to point out to the minister that, as the system is* working at present, it is actually making it impossible to fulfil that primary consideration. As was pointed out just a moment ago by the hon. member for Calgary East, in actual practice men with a higher number of points but with less overseas service, and certainly with less combat service, are coming back, while men who have been away from Canada longer, who have seen more action in a theatre of operations, are being left over there. So that the point system is actually defeating the very purpose the minister said it was incorporated to achieve.
In view of these facts I suggest that the minister can have no alternative but to agree to change that system. He gave us figures to show that of those personnel returned in the month of September a very large proportion were high-point men. Nevertheless, those figures do not present an accurate picture of the number of men with long overseas service who have been returned to Canada, because I repeat, the point system as it is now in operation gives more points to men with less service overseas and less service in a theatre of operations than to men who have had more overseas or actual combat service. Therefore included with the personnel having high-point scores under the present system there were large numbers of troops, as we have been told, who have been returned 
after having seen no action and with only a very short time overseas. In view of the fact that this system is defeating the very purpose for which it was designed; in view of the fact that it is achieving the result of bringing back a large number of men with short overseas service, I suggest that on his own statements the minister can have no alternative but to find some change in the point system.
As to administrative difficulties, reference already has been made to the rotational leave system, and I can assure the minister that he underestimates the ability of the officers of the first and second echelons overseas if he thinks they cannot cope with the administrative difficulties involved in redesigning the point system along the lines which have- been suggested in this house to-night, although I do not say those suggestions have been worked out in detail. That rotational leave S3rstem had assumed very large proportions just before the end of the war in Europe; yet echelon was still able to produce, in some fifteen days, complete lists of priority for the whole army on the information it had available. If they could do that, then most certainly if given the principles on which to work they could redesign the point system. So that I repeat, in- view of the objectives which the minister stated were in mind when the point system was designed; in view of the fact that it is defeating those objectives; in view of the fact that it is working injustices, and in view of the fact -that there is no serious administrative difficulty in the way of redesigning it, I say he should live up to the motives which I know exist in his heart, and for which I give him credit. Let him give those motives free play, then, and allow this system to be redesigned.

Evidence has been produced here to-night coming from every province. Perhaps I have had more letters than most hon. members, because the units which have returned to Canada so far are those which I had the great honour of commanding when I went overseas with the first Canadian division. I do not -think I am exaggerating when I say I have had letters from men of every single, unit of that first division, which is now back, and from every part of the country: The Royal Canadian Regiment from London; the 48th from Toronto; the Hastings and Prince Edward from Belleville. The Second Brigade came from western Canada; the Edmonton Regiment from Edmonton, Alberta; the Seaforths from Vancouver and the Princess Patricia Canadian Light Infantry from Winnipeg. The Third Brigade came frorfr the maritimes and Quebec-the Royal 22nd, from Quebec; the West Nova Scotia

Demobilization-Army
Regiment from Nova Scotia and the Carleton and York from New Brunswick. In addition to that, were the Princess Louise Dragoon Guards from Ottawa, and the Saskatoon Light Infantry from Saskatchewan.
I have heard from all those regiments, and * they tell me the same story. I am here to-night pleading for my soldiers, pleading for the men who went over with me in 1939, and who were followed very quickly by other units from all over Canada. They feel-and I do, too-that the present point system is not working out satisfactorily, and that it is giving too much preference to those men who served-perhaps by mere chance-for a longer time in Canada. Therefore, in the face of all this evidence which has been produced I ask the minister this question: Will he or will he not now revise the point system?

I do not propose to continue the discussion on the point system, which has been severely criticized by hon. members on this side of the house who have seen service in this war and who are thoroughly familiar with that subject. From the letters I have received and from what has been said here to-day it is clear to me that the system is not satisfactory and has resulted in injustices.
I wish, however, to direct the minister's thoughts to other matters. He has informed us that it is the intention of the government to have, after the war, a permanent army of from 20,000 to 25,000 men. I rise to express the hope that he will see his way clear to have part of that force stationed in New Brunswick.
I believe that, on strategic grounds, and for other very good reasons, they should be stationed there. At one time Saint John and Fredericton were garrison towns; British units were stationed in both places, and the dominion government to-day owns land in both Saint John and Fredericton, and buildings which were formerly occupied by those troops, and could be used again. Those properties could be made available for part of the new Canadian army.
I am asking the minister to have part of that new army stationed in New Brunswick. Perhaps the matter has already been brought to his attention, because I have received resolutions passed by the Saint John board of trade and by the city council dealing with the subject. The one from the board of trade is as follows:
Whereas it is proposed to establish in Canada a peace-time regular army of approximately 25,00'0 men and
Whereas there are at Saint John and Fredericton in this province on land owned
by federal authorities adequate barracks facilities which, at a small expense, could be made into permanent quarters-
Therefore be it resolved that the department of national defence be urged to station at both Saint John and Fredericton at least one unit of the proposed army.
Another reason for making this request is that it will provide some business for that part of Canada. Canadian industry is to a great extent centralized in Ontario and Quebec. New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces are badly in need of more industries, and if they cannot get more industries they are badly in need of more business in order to provide employment for their people.
The Rowell-Sirois commission stated in its report that New Brunswick shared with Nova Scotia the unhappy distinction of having the most unfavourable economic history of any Canadian province. I regret to say that statement is true, and it has resulted in a most unsatisfactory state of affairs. Early in the war when the government was spending many millions of dollars to establish industries in different parts of Canada I asked that some of those industries be established1 in New Brunswick. However, the government did not see its way clear to follow my suggestion, I do not think I am making an unreasonable request when I ask the minister and the government to see to it that some of the troops of the new Canadian army are stationed in Saint John and Fredericton.

I should like to say a few words, not on the point system and not as a returned man or a veteran. I wish to speak a few words on behalf of Prince Edward Island, and the war veterans of that province. Someone has already said that every province had spoken; apparently it was forgotten that the voice of Prince Edward Island had not been heard.
I do not believe the minister will take offence to any of the remarks I shall make. If he does, then I will say he misinterprets what I shall say. I desire to place before the committee the unfair, unjust and shameful treatment meted out to the service men of my province by the Department of National Defence of this government. I refer to what has been done in connection with the service men returning home for demobilization, Like one of the other speakers. I make no apology for making these complaints, nor do I apologize for charging this department for the treatment it has handed out to our service men.
About October 15 I asked certain questions, and received the answers regarding our service men. Those questions had to do with

I hope I shall be pardoned for speaking a second time on this item, but I am astonished that the minister has not as yet answered the question which the hon. member for Nanaimo asked him point-blank just before he concluded his remarks.
The hon. member for Regina City, speaking this evening, brought forth some facts which have been a problem with me since the beginning of this war, indicating as they do that we have an overorganized, overexpanded army in Canada in respect of high ranking officers. I can recall, session after session, questioning one of the ministers of defence, who was let out a year ago this fall, on that very topic, but I always thought somebody else was responsible for this overorganization of the
Canadian army and the creation of so many high ranking positions. The man who, rightly or wrongly, I blame for that is the predecessor of the present minister of this department. It was pointed out by the hon. member for Regina City that we now have enough officers to man fully some seven divisions, and enough other ranks for probably half a division. I wonder whether the taxpayers of this country realize what it will cost them for many years in the future to have so many high ranking officers to man an army which this nation could not possibly reinforce in time of battle. Naturally many of these officers will receive handsome retiring allowances when the time comes, for which the taxpayers of this country will be called upon to pay. To me that is a very improper thing, no matter who is responsible. I repeat that, frankly, it was always my opinion that the minister's predecessor was responsible for this overorganization, and certainly it was always the responsibility of the government. The final responsibility, in war and in peace, rests on parliament and, in this case, on the minister of this department.
I have been amazed to hear during the discussion this afternoon and this evening the repeated statement of the minister that he is satisfied with the recommendation of the officers overseas in this matter, because ultimately it is his responsibility and that of his colleagues in the government. There can be no argument about that at all. I do not deny that General Simmonds is a fine officer and a good soldier, but it is to be remembered that he is the officer responsible for the dismissal of Major Macfarlane from the position of editor of the Maple Leaj because he criticized the repatriation policy which is now in effect, a policy which is most unfair, and the minister himself admits that it unfair and that he does not like it in any respect.

Goes to Chungking. Edmonton, October 29.-[DOT] (CP)-Squadron Leader Chester Ronning of Gamrose, former provincial leader of the C.C.F. left Edmonton Saturday for New York where he will fly to China to take up an appointment at the Canadian embassy in Chungking.

We are now wondering whether hon. members opposite will get together with the leader of the C.C.F., the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and select one of these envoys for Tokyo. An hon. member says that one of the parties might be prejudiced in favour of the Japanese. Speaking seriously, I wish to say that with most of what the member for Nanaimo said the other day I agree. I do not approve the present system. I believe the system we shoidd have set up was "first in, first out" from start to finish. But I wish to point out this. Who were the people who objected about two weeks ago to the system of "first in, first, out?" Who were the people who objected to men being brought home on exceptional compassionate grounds?
I do not approve the policy of this government in not discharging men to go back to their own employmenV-not to take some new job but to go back to their own employment or their own business. It is foolish to keep them in when the men are needed on farms and in essential industries. I do not approve the policy of the government in allowing N.R.M.A. or any other men with short-time service overseas to be brought home ahead of others with long service. But I would point out to. you, Mr. Chairman, that there is no one in this house, there is no party, that has emphasized more the advantage of the Minister of National Defence taking advice from responsible officers than the Conservative party in this house have done.
No one can accuse me of sticking up for these high ranking officers. There are so many of them here that you cannot walk down Elgin street unless you go down the middle of the street, because you will bump into generals, colonels and everything else. But they are not walking; as I said the other day; they are driven by C.W.A.C.'s.
The minister is a fair man and he will try to devise some scheme whereby at least exceptional compassionate cases can be dealt with. I do not believe in citing individual cases, but I might mention one in my own 
riding. An old gentleman, seventy-eight years of age, is trying to keep the farm going for his grandson, but he will have to. dispose of. that farm. He has been trying to save the farm and the stock for that boyr who has a long point record and who is still overseas. Two miles away on another farm an N.R.M.A. man has arrived back with a very low point record. How can I explain to people in my district this discrepancy between one man who has a few points and who did not go over there voluntarily but is now home on his farm, and the other boy who cannot get home and whose grandfather is trying his best to run the farm.
I agree with the opposition on the matter of the point system. I do not often agree with them, and when I do they must be right or I would not agree with them. The reason I do not agree with them oftener is that they are generally wrong. However, I agree that the minister should reconsider the question. I am going to leave the point system, and the bringing of men home, to the minister, because I am perfectly sure that, having heard the voice of Fraser Valley, he will consider the matter and make it a better system.
I wish to speak on some of .the things that I think the Department of National Defence should be doing and are not doing. For instance, if we are to be successful in our victory loan we have to show to the people of Canada that we are legitimately and honestly trying to economize. Here again I do not agree with the opposition when they ask us to increase our standing army, navy and air force. The hon. member for York South who made way for a man who did not make headway in a by-election wants us to curtail expenditures all the time and yet increase our army, navy and other war expenditures. You cannot do both. You have either to curtail your army and your other expenditures or you cannot cut down on the expenditure of money. Personally I am not in a position to say what the size of our standing army, navy and air force should be. I have not the ability and knowledge possessed by one or two members of the official opposition who have such complete knowledge of military affairs that they set themselves up at least as the leaders of the military in this or any other country.
I do not know what the size of the standing army should be, but I do think our own Department of National Defence should pay heed to General Crerar. We had enough confidence in General Crerar to entrust him with the Canadian army; therefore, we should have confidence in his judgment as to what standing army we should have in Canada.

speechtext: It was not changed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I have dealt with this point three or four times already. In introducing these estimates I made a carefully considered statement, and I will quote to my hon. friend what I said at that time. I made quite an extended statement then on the repatriation policy, and I made a rather shorter, simpler statement in answer to the hon. member for Nanaimo a week or so before that. As the hon. member himself admitted, no policy can stick rigidly to the principle of "first in, first out". It just does not work. The hon. member was one of the first to admit that. Here is what I said, as reported at page 1131 of Hansard:
The common principle underlying the whole scheme of demobilization has always been, and in future will continue to be that subject to the exigencies of the service and to the national interests, the personnel with the longest and

hardest service should be given first opportunity to return to civil life. However, the loose description of this as a policy of "first in-first out" is somewhat misleading, as it ignores the two essential qualifications to which the main principle has always been subject. It is inevitable that there should occasionally occur some combination of circumstances or unusual conditions wherein a general policy becomes inapplicable, or wherein an exception must be made. In such an event the interests of Canada or of the majority of personnel directly concerned must, in the final instance, receive preference over the single person or minor group affected. The circumstances must always be viewed as a whole-and judgment cannot be correctly passed in the light of a single factor or isolated incident.
Both before and after that I discussed in somewhat more detail the application of the principle. In reply to the hon. member for Nanaimo I pointed out exceptions to the general rule regarding the longest and hardest service: compassionate grounds, which have always existed; releases under recommendations of the industrial release and assignment board, and the like. That has all been, gone over time and again. There is no uncertainty as to what the policy is; I do not think there ever has been any uncertainty. It may be right or wrong, but the policy is clear enough.

, I followed the remarks of the minister and I read them in Hansard. In making those remarks the minister, being a member of the legal profession, always used a legal manner. I do not object to that at all, but I would point out that in this little pamphlet which was presented to the boys overseas, which I have never seen and which I doubt if any other hon. member has ever seen, it was probably set out in a very simple manner and was not clothed in any of the legal terms or expressions the minister has just read from Hansard. That is one of the things I am objecting to, because, as this article well points out, the men accepted it in good faith. Everyone accepted it in good faith, because it went on to set out the manner in which the men would be repatriated. It was to be simply a question of priority; those who had been in the service longest would be the first released.
The minister has suggested that if any h'on. member knows of a man who has a high-point score and who feels himself discriminated against, all he has to do is to bring the matter to the minister's attention. That is very generous, but as another hon. member pointed out there are thousands and thousands of men in the army. They cannot all write to their members of parliament, and after all, as I have said on other occasions in this house when talking about pension matters, it should never be necessary for any

Demobilization-Army
soldier to write to his member of parliament in order to get something which is his by right. If the policy is that the first in shall 'be the first out, or if the policy is that the man with the highest point score is to be the first man out, then the men should get the benefit of that without having to write to their members of parliament, without requiring any political pull or anything else.
In speaking of the various units which had been under his command, the -hon. member for Nanaimo mentioned the famous Hastings and Prince Edward regiment which recently returned to Canada. This was one of the regiments which left Canada in December, 1939. It had a very high percentage of casualties, and no doubt the same procedure was followed in this as in all other cases, that when reinforcements were required they were obtained in the usual way. Naturally, when that regiment came home very few of the originals were left, but there were a great many men who had been with the regiment for only a very short time, some who had joined it as late as just before V-E day and others who had joined even after V-E day. Yet these men with very low point scores, although no doubt more than the fifty points which the minister said was the minimum, were returned to Canada, while many men who had belonged to the Hastings and Prince Edward regiment are retained in the army of occupation in what are called key or essential positions.
I can only reiterate what other hon. members have said and ask the minister if he will not reconsider the whole matter; and, as was suggested by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, forget all about the advice of his brass hats. Let the minister use his own common sense and judgment. He was an ordinary rear ranker in the last war, and if he will only use his own judgment I am satisfied he will change the present system.

I could not say. I have
not seen that article, but only two pamphlets have been issued, this one and one issued two or three weeks ago by General Simmonds, or at any rate by overseas authorities. I have a few copies of the second pamphlet here. I do not know that I have enough as yet to make a general distribution, but certainly I will table one or -two so tha-t any hon. member may look at it. It does not change the principle; it merely elaborates on the first pamphlet.

I
think it is the one printed in May we are interested in.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I think so. I should like
to read paragraph 19:
Like most other things in this war, the scaling-down of the army will be a question of priority. Speaking generally, the principle upon which priorities will be based is that those with the longest service in- the army will be the first to be released. Priority for individual release will be established by a point score system explained below.
Then it goes on to explain the way in which the system works. I should like also to read paragraph 26, which after mentioning the ordinary way in which the point score is figured out, goes on to say:
26.	There are other things, however, to consider besides the feelings or even the entitlement of the individual. In general those with the highest priority will be released for return to Canada, but normal services must be maintained throughout the army during the reallocation period and there may be adjustments between corps as to the individual priority required to qualify for inclusion in the first groups to be released. For instance, it by chance a great number of R.C.A.S.C. personnel all had the highest possible priority, they could not all be released immediately as the army would then not be able to function efficiently.
27.	Then again it is bound to be the case that a much larger proportion of officers- commissioned, warrant and non-commissioned- will have higher priorities than will private soldiers, as. in general, such officers having come up through the ranks, their longer service is inevitable. On the other hand, the overruling necessity of maintaining efficient organization and administration throughout the Canadian army will prevent the release of officers other than in approximate proportion to the numbers of private soldiers.



Demobilization-Army

Then the expansion of the system of return of units, interspersed with Canada drafts, and so on, is gone into. That is the pamphlet which was issued overseas early in May, and I think it must be the one to which the hon. member has referred. In any event a supply will be available to-morrow for hon. members who may be interested.

The minister said he had replied to my question two or three times. I am afraid he must have been under some misapprehension, because he did not speak after I had asked my question, except in reply to the hon. member for Peterborough West.
There was one essential difference. I asked this: Would the minister revise the point system now, in view of the evidence which had been presented to him showing that there was general dissatisfaction, and also the evidence offered by the hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard to the effect that the difficulties he saw in the way of revising the point system could be overcome by the very simple method of allotting a bonus to those men wearing campaign medals? That seems to be the simplest way in which it could be done.
We are all perfectly familiar with the impossibility of following exactly the principle of "first-in, first-out". Everyone has admitted that there must be exceptions to that rule. We all know about compassionate leave, and that sort of thing, and we accept that situation. But the fundamental injustice, that the point system does not give adequate points to the man who has had the longest and the most hazardous service, remains. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has offered a simple solution, namely, that of allotting an additional point to those wearing a campaign medal. Will the minister answer that simple question? Will he or will he not revise the points system, with that in view?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am not going to answer any such simple question. I will submit the suggestion made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard to the staff, and I shall consider it. But, as I said before, this question is not so simple as all that. What my hon. friend has chosen to call evidence consists of assertions by himself and by some other hon. members. They may or may not be true.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
But let me say that that is not evidence. I can assert, with equal assurance, and with all sincerity, that I have had statements from friends of mine who have returned and who consider that the system is
perfectly satisfactory. It is a matter of opinion and, as I said earlier, it involves the exercise of judgment on the part of someone. The person who finally has to exercise that judgment is my unfortunate self. I have to take the advice of the military advisers whom I have to advise me. As I said earlier in the debate, if I am not prepared to accept their advice, I should replace them. Until they tell me that they are prepared to recommend another system, and so long as they have my confidence as minister I, as minister, am not going to override their decision. I cannot say anything further than that, and I have said that already two or three times to-day.
But the minister 'will have the matter reviewed again?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, of course. I have also given that assurance two or three times. It is being under constant review.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No; this item cannot carry. Will the minister bring down to-morrow complete figures showing the present disposition of N.R.M.A. troops both overseas and in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes; I do not know whether I shall be able to give all the information to-morrow. However, I think I have complete figures for Canada, and I think I should be able to give them for overseas, too. If I do not have them to-morrow, then I will have them next day.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
